The resultant structures can be secured through the solidification of the surrounding medium. Unlike existing approaches, this technique works with matter that exhibits positive acoustic contrast and doesn't need opposing sound waves, supporting surfaces or frameworks. The potential applications of this method in tissue engineering and additive manufacturing are considerable.

There has been growing interest in automating medical evidence collection and diagnosis to ease doctors' workloads and make healthcare more accessible to everyone. However, research has largely focused on enhancing machine learning models' ability to predict patient diagnoses. This goal is insufficient to ensure doctors will accept and trust such systems. In their initial patient interactions, doctors don't just diagnose the patient's pathology; instead, they generate a differential diagnosis, which involves considering several potential diseases based on the limited evidence collected. Moreover, doctors first investigate severe pathologies, even if they might later be ruled out, especially in emergency settings. To gain doctors' trust, a system's recommendations need to be transparent and explain how it arrived at its conclusions. This means system-patient interactions should mirror doctors' thought processes. We propose using a deep reinforcement learning framework to model evidence collection and automatic diagnosis tasks, incorporating three key elements of a doctor's reasoning. Our framework involves generating a differential diagnosis using an exploratory approach while prioritizing critical pathologies, and we introduce metrics to assess the quality of system-patient interactions based on these aspects. Our approach outperforms existing models in certain aspects, maintaining a competitive level of pathology prediction accuracy.

In the field of drug discovery, water solubility is a key pharmacokinetic attribute that influences how a drug is absorbed and made available for testing. To improve virtual screening and lead optimization, researchers have been exploring in-silico prediction of solubility, particularly through machine learning methods that utilize experimental data. While machine learning techniques have gained popularity due to their efficiency in high-throughput tasks, they can suffer from over-fitting in cases of limited data and are often difficult to interpret. To address these challenges, we have developed a Bayesian graph neural network with a self-attention readout layer, which enhances predictive performance and allows for the identification of individual atomic contributions. This model also enables the separation of reliable and uncertain results based on the uncertainty associated with solubility predictions. As a result, our model is expected to provide a more reliable foundation for informed decision-making and a range of applications in the development of medications.

Galactic haloes are likely composed of dark matter particles that would emit high-energy cosmic rays upon annihilation or decay. This talk will focus on antimatter species, which are extremely rare and should be easily identifiable if present in excess. Following a review of how particles propagate through the galaxy, I will discuss anomalies observed in positrons, antiprotons, and anti-nuclei. In particular, the antiproton anomaly has garnered significant attention but is no longer considered a compelling phenomenon once theoretical and data-related errors are properly accounted for.

We propose a method to refine the calibration score by integrating nearby forecasts to gauge a forecaster's proficiency, which is achievable through deterministic processes, ensuring smooth calibration even when forecasts are compromised or leaked. This method contrasts with regular calibration methods that are only guaranteed with randomized forecasting procedures. Our procedure also exhibits finite recall and is stationary, with forecasts being finite grid values. In addition, we address related concepts, such as online linear regression and weak calibration, to establish the procedure's robustness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this refined calibration yields uncoupled, finite-memory dynamics in n-person games, enabling "smooth calibrated learning" where players achieve approximate Nash equilibria in most periods, whereas calibrated learning results in approximate correlated equilibria time-averages.

Multi-robot motion planning is a complex task involving the creation of safe paths for a group of robots within a continuous environment. As the number of robots increases, the likelihood of collisions grows, particularly in confined spaces like warehouses. In single-robot settings, guided motion planning has shown improved performance in congested areas, leading us to adapt this approach for multiple robots by introducing topological guidance for the entire space. Our method effectively generates efficient routes in complex settings with multiple narrow pathways, handling teams significantly larger than comparable methods. By utilizing topological knowledge, we achieve better solution quality compared to other approaches.

In this paper, we present an innovative approach to simulating the Vlasov-Poisson system, utilizing a Local Macroscopic Conservative (LoMaC) method with a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretization scheme. The LoMaC property guarantees the precise local conservation of mass, momentum, and energy at the discrete level, which is achieved through a kinetic flux vector splitting and a projection onto a subspace with shared macroscopic observables. Building on our previous research, this paper generalizes the approach by incorporating DG discretization to leverage its compactness, flexibility in handling boundary conditions, and superior accuracy in long-term simulations. By treating the DG method as a nodal scheme, we can develop an algorithm that involves deriving differentiation matrices and defining a weighted inner product space, allowing for the extension to high-dimensional problems using hierarchical Tucker decomposition and conservative projection. Additionally, the algorithm can be adapted to various types of discretizations, such as the spectral method in the velocity direction, and is demonstrated through extensive numerical results to showcase its efficacy.

This paper views Dungeons and Dragons as an ideal test case for evaluating dialogue system capabilities by focusing on two key tasks: generating the next turn in a conversation and accurately predicting the game's state based on the dialogue history. A comprehensive dataset of nearly 900 games, involving over 7,000 players, 800,000 turns, 500,000 dice rolls, and 58 million words, has been compiled and annotated with partial game information. A large language model has been trained to produce coherent game dialogue, capable of adopting the voice of specific characters or the game master, while also generating in-character or out-of-character dialogue. Human evaluation has been conducted to assess factors contributing to plausible and engaging output, while automatic evaluation has been used to examine the model's capacity to forecast the game state and determine how accurately tracking the state enhances the model's conversational performance.

A novel particle tracking velocimetry device has been developed to track three-dimensional particle paths within vast areas, up to several meters in size, during snowfall events. This device was utilized in outdoor experiments during the 2021/2022 winter season to study the motion of snow particles in atmospheric flows. Initial findings from these experiments are presented. The methodology behind the research, which incorporates a calibration method based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) technology, is outlined, along with an analysis of a selected dataset that demonstrates the capabilities of the system for examining particle dynamics within atmospheric flows. The camera array, designed for deployment in challenging weather conditions, captures synchronized images of a target attached to a UAV, enabling the collection of precise measurements within a 4 m x 4 m x 6 m volume 10 m above the ground. Using data from particle trajectories, we present statistical information regarding particle path curvature and acceleration, as well as clustering patterns observed through Voronoi analysis. Limitations of this system and potential future improvements are discussed in the context of its application to the study of other types of particles subject to inertial forces.

This research introduces a new mathematical operator that plays a crucial role in understanding and controlling flows in systems operating under consistent conditions far from their standard, unchanging state. The'mean resolvent' $\mathbf{R}_0$ is a mathematical tool used to forecast how systems respond to stimuli in the frequency domain. It provides the most accurate linear approximation of the complex dynamics of systems and has been studied in the context of repetitive patterns. The operator's properties have been explored and found to be closely related to a system's fundamental characteristics, including its stability. A key finding of this study is that, under certain conditions, the average system response to multiple stimuli can be predicted without actually averaging the responses. This concept is referred to as 'dynamic linearity.' For systems that are slightly changing over time but not rapidly, the'mean resolvent' $\mathbf{R}_{0}$ is very similar to a well-known operator, $\mathbf{R}_{\overline{\mathbf{U}}}$. Although the research in this paper only applies to systems that exhibit periodic patterns, the concept of the'mean resolvent' remains relevant for understanding complex flows, such as those found in turbulent systems, which have a diverse range of patterns. Numerical simulations demonstrate the close relationship between $\mathbf{R}_0$ and $\mathbf{R}_{\overline{\mathbf{U}}}$ in various types of systems, including those with chaotic and random patterns.

Forecast accuracy is measured by comparing predictions to actual results. 
Our approach introduces the concept of forecast hedging, where predictions are chosen to ensure only positive performance. 
This leads to all calibration results through a unified reasoning, distinguishing between them by the tools employed: 
deterministic and fixed point versus stochastic and minimax based methods. 
Further advancements include a refined definition of continuous calibration, resulting game dynamics, 
and a novel, simpler calibrated forecasting technique for binary events.

In a recent study by Rusciano et al., the statistics of individual particles' movements in two-dimensional glass-forming materials showed a non-Gaussian distribution in a timeframe where the mean-squared displacement adhered to Fickian behavior. However, we point out that the study's multiple length and time scales have either been previously established or remain unclear. This ambiguity leads us to challenge the conclusions that glass-formers exhibit Fickian non-Gaussian behavior, and we also question whether this analogy provides a useful explanation for the underlying dynamics of heterogeneity in these systems.

Investigating a linear polymer in a solvent, we analyze the statistical behavior of its conformations, allowing for the formation of double polymers. Utilizing a classical method to develop a field theory from an O(n) symmetric spin model, we derive a model applicable to RNA or DNA with constant monomer binding energy. A stable renormalization group fixed point is demonstrated, where the double polymer separates from the single-strand polymer and evolves into a branched polymer with a three-point interaction. This occurs after adjusting one or more parameters, with the system exhibiting a critical dimension of eight. Upon reaching this point, the Fisher-renormalization, equation of state, and critical exponents for both single-strand and double-strand polymers are replicated.

In the realm of biomedicine, antibodies stand out as the most diverse class of binding molecules. For the development of therapeutic antibodies, it's crucial to design new sequences with superior properties while maintaining structural coherence. Recent advancements in language models and graph neural networks have significantly improved antibody sequence generation. However, the limited availability of known antibody structures poses a challenge, often leading to decreased performance and a lack of diversity in generated samples. To mitigate this issue, we're employing Model Reprogramming, a technique that redeploys pre-trained machine learning models to tackle tasks with scarce data. This involves reprogramming pre-trained natural language models to fill in protein sequence templates as a means of creating novel proteins. For designing variable CDR sequences, we've adapted text infilling using an antibody's constant region as the sequence template. Our reprogrammed model achieved outstanding results on antibody design benchmarks, yielding highly diverse CDR sequences with a notable two-fold increase over baseline models, all while preserving structural integrity and naturalness. The performance benefits of the reprogrammed model became particularly apparent when designing longer CDR sequences or infilling multiple loops simultaneously, outperforming existing graph-based models that require additional structural information. Furthermore, the generated sequences demonstrated enhanced antigen binding specificity and virus neutralization capabilities.

The development of comprehensive and informative datasets plays a crucial role in supporting research and innovation across various scientific disciplines. Assembling large datasets, however, can be a complex task that requires careful consideration and coordination among researchers and stakeholders. In this paper, we outline the challenges and opportunities we encountered during the creation of a European agricultural dataset featuring labeled information on cultivated crops, aiming to provide a useful guide for those who aim to create their own datasets.

A Gaussian Process-based surrogate model inherently addresses anomalies stemming from data limitations, gaps, inconsistencies and inaccuracies within digital twin modeling, specifically in accident tolerant fuel (ATF) concepts. Nevertheless, its accuracy declines when relying on limited high-fidelity data. Moreover, handling high-dimensional functions is challenging for GP, particularly when dealing with over 20-dimensional functions, whereas noisy data poses a significant obstacle for advanced ATF concepts. Additionally, data scarcity and empirical governing differential equations exacerbate these challenges. However, physics-informed multi-fidelity Kriging (MFK) is particularly beneficial for identifying required material properties and can effectively cope with low-fidelity physics and limited high-fidelity data. This is crucial in ATF development where data availability is scarce. This chapter delves into the application of the MFK method on experimental thermal conductivity data for ATF candidates, demonstrating its significance even with limited data. The constructed models can be seamlessly integrated with subsequent analysis such as uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, the overarching aim is to demonstrate the potential of embedding MFK-based surrogates into digital twin systems for accident tolerant fuel (ATF).

A universal method for simplifying systems using various interpretations of Dirac's work is devised, encompassing a broad category that includes Poisson maps, and this process recovers several fundamental concepts in Poisson and quasi-Poisson geometry. This technique is utilized to establish a novel method for simplifying quasi-Poisson systems based on the action of a specific subgroup category. Furthermore, it leads to the identification of quasi-Poisson structures in several types of spaces studied within geometric representation theory.

Single atoms are gaining attention for potential use in quantum optics and quantum information processing due to recent advancements in their trapping and manipulation using tight optical dipole traps. We investigate the behavior of atoms in a specially designed optical dipole trap with an inverted beam direction and observe a significant increase in two-atom collision rates of six times. Our theoretical model forecasts a high likelihood of loading a small number of atoms into the trap under ideal experimental conditions. This study presents a novel method for controlling the behavior of a few atoms in a dipole trap and exploring the collective quantum effects that occur when few atoms interact.

This paper explores the quantization of a model introduced by Carlip, showcasing an innovative approach to relating boundary degrees of freedom to the stretched horizon of a stationary black hole. Similar to JT gravity, this concept associates boundary freedom with non-extremal black holes. A path integral is formed, now encompassing the integration of time reparametrizations on the stretched horizon, keeping its length constant. These degrees of freedom can be seen as elements of $Diff(S^1)/S^1$, essentially coadjoint orbits under the Virasoro group's action. By deriving the symplectic form on this manifold, the measure for the boundary path integral is determined. After a one-loop computation centered around the classical solution, a non-finiteness issue arises, suggesting potential instability or an action problem akin to quantum gravity's conformal mode issue. Following an analytic continuation of the field, the boundary partition function obtained is independent of inverse temperature and does not contribute to thermodynamics, at least within one-loop calculations. This stands in contrast to near-extremal black hole studies using JT gravity, where boundary freedom is the sole contributor to thermodynamic properties.

A common issue with multilingual models is their poor performance on low-resource languages due to these languages being underrepresented in their training data. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new training technique that leverages teacher-student knowledge distillation in a multilingual context. Specifically, we employ individually optimized teacher models for each language and utilize a balanced subset of their training data to distill their knowledge into a single multilingual model. This innovative approach surpasses conventional training methods in low-resource languages while also retaining performance on high-resource languages when working with the same amount of data. If broadly adopted, our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the representation of low-resource languages in NLP systems.

Microresonators have profoundly impacted modern nonlinear and quantum optics by enabling frequency conversion. We've developed a theory for multimode second harmonic generation in microresonators where parametric conversion to the pump spectrum occurs prominently across a broad range of resonator parameters. This regime's sideband spectral tunability is determined by discrete Eckhaus instability sequences. We've observed the transition to modelocking and the generation of solitons, specifically those with double-pulse structures in the pump field existing on a curved background outside bistability intervals.

The electrical conductivity through single-layer and bilayer graphene junctions is determined, taking into account the influence of band gap and bias voltage. Initially, we examine graphene with an existing band gap and then connect it to pristine bilayer graphene. When the Fermi energy exceeds the interlayer hopping energy, two distinct models of anti-resonances appear, both with the same periodicity, as a function of bilayer region length. The conductivity profile reveals that for bilayer graphene with AA stacking, band gaps produce identical minima, regardless of the region length, while AB stacking creates a global energy gap that depends on this length. Next, we consider pristine single-layer graphene connected to biased bilayer graphene. In this configuration, peaks in the conductivity appear with varying periods and shapes, along with Klein tunneling that yields zero conductivity, unlike the first setup. Additionally, for very short lengths (less than 10), conductivity vanishes, resulting in anti-Klein tunneling as the Fermi energy changes. We also investigate the conductivity as a function of applied bias. For AA-stacked bilayer graphene, anti-resonances occur and decrease for large bias values, regardless of the bilayer region length. However, AB-stacked bilayer graphene exhibits unique characteristics, including initial conductivity with maxima at low Fermi energy and minima at high Fermi energy.

SOLNP+ is a derivative-free optimization tool designed for solving constrained nonlinear problems. Building on the SOLNP approach introduced in 1989 by Ye Ye, this updated version utilizes finite differences to approximate gradients and incorporates recent advancements such as implicit filtering, improved restart mechanisms, and high-performance quadratic programming solvers. Notably, SOLNP+ boasts enhanced efficiency and stability under noisy conditions compared to its predecessor. This software is freely available for download at https://github.com/COPT-Public/SOLNP_plus.

A novel portfolio strategy is developed that dynamically adjusts to changing market information, offering a universal wealth guarantee when compared to traditional rebalanced portfolios, provided the changing market data can be mapped into a finite set of market conditions. Specifically, when a set of possible market scenarios is finite and limited, the new strategy is shown to perform as well as the best traditional rebalanced portfolio strategy, with this level of performance achieved to the greatest degree when looking back on the market's actual behavior.

A cutting-edge medical imaging method called photoacoustic tomography (PAT) employs non-ionizing laser pulses to produce acoustic waves within the subject, which are detected and translated into images of the body. In this context, solving a specific mathematical problem involves retrieving the initial signal from the solution of a wave equation obtained outside the subject. Our research focuses on the fractional wave equation, under the assumption that detectors are placed on the surface of a sphere or a plane. We outline the procedure for determining the initial signal from data collected from the solution of the fractional wave equation measured on a sphere and a plane.

Trans-Neptunian objects and Centaurs in the outer solar system exhibit
distinct photometric characteristics, which are influenced by their changing
orientation. By utilizing absolute photometry and rotational light-curves at
various orbital positions, researchers can develop detailed models that reveal
key properties such as axial tilt, physical shape, and density. Furthermore,
these models can also uncover anomalies, like deviations from hydrostatic
equilibrium or the presence of rings. This work outlines the methodology for
creating such models and presents a comprehensive review of existing research
on objects with long-term photometric behavior that has been successfully
modeled.

A cutting-edge Optical Wireless Communication system known as Visible Light Communication has been recognized for its reliability and ability to provide secure line-of-sight, short-range vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communications. To enhance the dependability of self-driving cars, researchers have suggested that V2I connections, which are supported by automated driving applications, can provide significant improvements. With the goal of increasing the communication redundancy of self-driving valet parking systems, we propose a VLC-based V2I system that leverages the unique properties of VLC, including jam-free and location-based capabilities. This study presents a groundbreaking design for updating online parking maps in indoor parking garages through two-way VLC communication, allowing for the transmission and dissemination of vehicle data, camera footage, and other vital information. Our proposed system achieves flawless line-of-sight transmission at a distance of up to 33 meters, making it suitable for sharing vehicle data and other essential information within an indoor parking garage setting.

Over the past decade, 3D graphics have become incredibly realistic but highly demanding, making them challenging to process due to their size and complexity. To achieve the optimal Quality of Experience (QoE), it is essential to evaluate the visual quality of these graphics to determine the right balance between their visual quality and the required data size. We focus on developing a method to assess the quality of 3D meshes with textures by creating a large dataset and leveraging it to design a learning-based quality metric. This metric outperforms existing approaches when evaluating textured meshes, as well as meshes with vertex colors. We also utilize our dataset and metric to investigate the impact of different distortions and content characteristics on the perceived quality of compressed 3D graphics. A comprehensive crowdsourced subjective experiment with over 4500 participants was conducted to evaluate 55 source models, which were distorted in various ways to produce over 343k stimuli. The results from this experiment enabled us to select a subset of the most challenging stimuli for quality evaluation.

A theoretical and computational framework grounded in fractional calculus has been developed to investigate the nonlocal response of curved cylindrical shells under static conditions. Fractional derivatives' inherent differ-integral properties enable a precise and efficient method to capture long-range interactions in complex structures, thereby yielding physically consistent models. By incorporating shell elements based on first-order shear-deformable theory into the fractional-Finite Element Method, this approach can simulate nonlocal elastic interactions under a range of practical loading scenarios. Through both linear and geometrically nonlinear static response analyses, numerical studies have been conducted to explore the nonlocal behavior of cylindrical shell panels, providing a foundational framework for the investigation of curved structures through fractional order models.

Standard and non-standard Lagrangians can generate the same dynamics, despite their distinct forms, as the latter lack recognizable energy-based terms. A specific group of these non-standard Lagrangians are termed null Lagrangians, accompanied by their gauge functions. Demonstrating that null Lagrangians can be used to incorporate dissipative forces into physical systems is a crucial finding. As conventional null Lagrangians have been linked to non-dissipative forces, the presented research provides an in-depth understanding of the novel roles played by null Lagrangians in introducing forces to dynamic systems. Furthermore, the research discusses its implications on Newton's laws and explores their Galilean invariance properties.

A comprehensive collection of machine learning articles, validated both through experimentation and computation, is categorized based on the size of the training data into three groups: 1-100, 101-10000, and over 10000. This compilation highlights the integration of synthesis, characterization, and prediction within the field, emphasizing the utilization of Bayesian optimization and support vector machines to varying degrees. Most articles leverage a combination of techniques including machine learning, feature selection, adaptive design, high-throughput methods, and domain expertise to enhance predictive accuracy and model interpretability. Cross-validation strategies are implemented to mitigate overly optimistic predictions, with smaller datasets using adaptive design to identify novel materials within constrained design spaces. In contrast, larger datasets tend to uncover low-hanging fruit in materials optimization, often struggling to extrapolate to new materials when training data favors a specific material type. The increasing number of machine learning materials science articles validating predicted results through experimentation or computation signifies a growing interconnection between materials informatics and the field of materials science, ultimately accelerating materials discovery for real-world applications.

The difficulties in developing retinal prostheses necessitate creating retinal models that accurately replicate the responses of Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs) to simulate real-world vision for the visually impaired. This paper proposes a functional assessment (FA) for evaluating retinal models' performance in visual recognition tasks. To achieve this, we employed machine learning algorithms that utilize RGC responses generated by retinal models to classify objects and digits from various datasets. Our investigation explored critical factors affecting FA, such as task dependency, optimal input processing, and the impact of output neuron count on accuracy. By experimenting with image segmentation and analyzing performance on different datasets, we discovered that neither method significantly enhances model accuracy. Furthermore, we found that variations in dataset structures yield disparate results, with certain datasets (MNIST and Fashion MNIST) achieving high accuracy (~80%), while others (CIFAR-10 and Imagenette) only achieved moderate success (~40%). Notably, retinal models that excel in standard evaluations also perform better in FA. Unlike traditional evaluations, FA outcomes provide straightforward insights into visual perception quality.

Reinforcement learning agents can benefit from knowledge transfer by leveraging insights from similar domains to facilitate learning in their target environments. A key area of research involves knowledge sharing between tasks with varying dynamics, reward functions, and most notably, action spaces. This paper addresses the knowledge transfer challenge across tasks with differing action spaces by introducing a reward shaping approach that utilizes source domain embedding similarity, capable of adapting to both discrete and continuous action spaces. We evaluated the effectiveness of our method in the context of action space restrictions within the Acrobot-v1 and Pendulum-v0 environments, where it demonstrated improved performance over two baselines in discrete action spaces, though it did not outperform them in continuous action spaces. Finally, we outline potential directions for further exploration in this area.

We observe that many real-world networks exhibit well-defined community structures, with nodes densely connected within each community. To effectively learn from such networks, we propose MarkovGNN, a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that directly captures community formation and evolution through distinct convolutional layers. Diverging from conventional GNNs that operate on static graphs, MarkovGNN leverages a Markov process to generate stochastic matrices for each layer, utilizing these community-capturing matrices to improve performance. Our framework is versatile and can be easily integrated with existing GNNs. Experimental results demonstrate MarkovGNN's superiority over other GNNs for clustering, classification, and visualization tasks. The source code for MarkovGNN is freely available online at https://github.com/HipGraph/MarkovGNN.

Developing assistive interfaces for controlling robots through various, high-dimensional inputs (such as eye gaze from webcam images) can be difficult, especially when inferring user actions without a default interface. To address this, leveraging online user feedback through reinforcement learning is a natural solution, allowing interfaces to adapt to individual users. However, this method requires a substantial amount of human-in-the-loop training data, especially when feedback is scarce. We propose a hierarchical approach that efficiently learns from sparse user feedback: first, we use offline pre-training to acquire a representation of useful high-level robot behaviors; subsequently, the system focuses on mapping user inputs to desired high-level behaviors through online learning. By having access to a pre-trained policy, the system can extract more information from sparse rewards: successful task executions are used to retroactively relabel what the user intended during unsuccessful executions. We evaluated our method through a user study with 12 participants who used a webcam and eye gaze in three simulated robotic manipulation domains, achieving results that show our approach effectively maps 128-dimensional gaze features to 7-dimensional joint torques in under 10 minutes of online training, and adapts to various user gaze strategies and distributional shifts in webcam inputs, tasks, and environments.

The study of red-giant stars in binary systems serves as an optimal means for understanding the complex processes governing the late stages of stellar evolution, given that 83 such systems have been discovered, with approximately 40 possessing well-established global seismic and orbital parameters. Typically, these systems are identified through the distinct signatures of binarity present in space-based photometry data, which often favors shorter orbital periods and smaller orbit sizes that enable full expansion of the red giant as it ascends the red-giant branch. Consequently, this sample is characterized by an overabundance of H-shell burning giants and a scarcity of stars in the He-core burning phase. Leveraging the ninth catalogue of spectroscopic binary orbits and conducting an exhaustive search through photometric data from various NASA missions and the BRITE constellation mission, 99 previously unknown systems hosting oscillating giant components have been identified. This expanded dataset, encompassing a wider range of orbital periods, up to 26000 days, provides an invaluable opportunity to explore the He-core burning primaries, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of stellar evolution through binary system studies. By effectively tripling the size of the known sample of oscillating red-giant stars in binary systems, researchers can now employ an ensemble approach for seismology and tidal studies, while the incorporation of Gaia astrometric orbits will unlock new avenues for investigation in the field of binary systems.

In network group testing applications, such as disease outbreak identification, leveraging correlations among nodes significantly reduces the number of required tests. We study group testing on a network with n nodes whose interactions are modeled by graph G. We introduce an edge-faulty random graph derived from G where each edge is dropped with probability 1-r and all nodes within the same component share the same state. Our analysis focuses on three network categories: cycles, trees, and d-regular graphs and stochastic block models, yielding lower and upper bounds for the number of tests required to identify defective nodes. These results express the number of tests in terms of n, r, and the target error rate, and reveal the extent of the improvement achieved by exploiting correlation in group testing. The lower bounds are established by illustrating the dependency of test numbers on the expected component size. We introduce a novel approximation for the distribution of component sizes in d-regular trees, leading to a new lower bound on the expected number of components in d-regular graphs. Conversely, upper bounds are achieved through dense subgraph construction where nodes are more likely to have the same state. When G is a cycle or tree, the correlation improvement is by a factor of log(1/r), while for grid graphs, the improvement is significantly greater at (1-r) log(1/r), and for larger-edge graphs such as SBM, the improvement can scale with n.

Our study presents an experimental analysis of the Doppler-free saturated absorption spectroscopy of buffer-gas-cooled Barium monofluoride (BaF) molecules within a 4 Kelvin cryogenic cell. The high-resolution spectra we achieved, with a resolution of nearly 19 MHz, far exceeding previous absorption spectroscopy results, have enabled the distinct separation of hyperfine transitions. By utilizing these detailed spectra, we were able to model the hyperfine splittings of the excited A(v=0) state and discovered that the hyperfine splitting of the A^2Π_(1/2)(v=0, J=1/2, +) state, relevant for laser cooling, is approximately 18 MHz. This finding, significantly higher than previously predicted, supplies critical missing information necessary for the laser cooling of BaF molecules.

Inverse problems are encountered across various fields including aerospace engineering and medical imaging, where the goal is to determine an underlying condition from available data. Solving these problems becomes particularly complex when forward models that produce these data are nonlinear and subject to randomness. A promising approach to addressing inverse problems is the use of neural networks, which can be trained with noisy data and operate efficiently once trained. However, neural networks used for inverse models lack inherent guarantees of correctness, making them unsuitable for applications requiring precision and reliability. This work introduces a method for validating the accuracy of neural networks used for inverse modeling. The approach involves approximating a complex forward model using simplified constraints and representing both the approximated model and the neural network as a mixed-integer program. We apply this verification procedure to a practical case study involving an airplane fuel gauge, thereby enabling the utilization of inverse model neural networks across various domains such as aerospace and medicine.

In established software development processes, determining a suitable code reviewer is a recognized challenge within the software engineering field. Assigning an inexperienced reviewer can hinder development and increase errors. Currently, most reviewer recommendation systems focus on historical data; those with prior involvement in a file's change or review are often selected for future reviews. However, this approach may overlook developers possessing the necessary expertise, even if they have never worked with a particular file before. To address this limitation, we introduce CORAL, a novel reviewer recommendation approach using a socio-technical graph of entities and relationships in source code management systems. Leveraging graph convolutional neural networks trained on two and a half years of history across 332 repositories, CORAL effectively models human reviewer selection decisions. Furthermore, our extensive user study reveals that CORAL identifies relevant and qualified reviewers often missed by traditional recommendation systems, and developers value their inclusion in the review process. Our findings suggest that classic reviewer recommenders perform well in smaller projects, whereas CORAL excels in larger projects, underscoring the need for tailored approaches.

In a scenario of sequential bargaining, we investigate the interactions between a proposer and a veto player who have single-peaked preferences but uncertain ideal points. The proposer's inability to commit to future proposals is a significant factor. When players are patient, the equilibrium can result in Coasian dynamics, with the veto player's private information diminishing the proposer's bargaining power. Our key finding reveals the existence of equilibria where the proposer achieves the highest possible payoff, akin to having commitment power. This outcome is driven by the veto player's single-peaked preferences, which enable the proposer to employ the strategy of "leapfrogging", by initially securing agreements with low-value types and subsequently credibly extracting value from high-value types. We use a novel methodological approach by linking sequential bargaining with static mechanism design.

Ensuring efficient wireless communication between devices is crucial, and scheduling schemes play a vital role. Conventional scheduling methods prioritize maximum throughput or fairness without considering information freshness. This paper presents a novel D2D scheduling scheme that optimizes both information age and network throughput under a packet-replacement policy. By jointly optimizing these performance metrics, it addresses the drawback of high-throughput scheduling, which can lead to poor information age. To model the scheduling problem, the paper derives an expression for the overall network performance under spatiotemporal queue dynamics. A neural network structure is proposed to learn the optimal scheduling parameters based on geographic location without requiring channel state information. To overcome the limitation of implicit loss functions, the paper develops a numerical solution for the gradient, enabling the optimization of scheduling parameters. The numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the deep learning approach, achieving performance close to that of a computationally complex local optimal algorithm. Furthermore, the trade-off between information age and network throughput is characterized, revealing that high throughput comes at the cost of increasing information age.

Recent findings indicate that when a specific type of non-negative definite kernel is applied to a complex domain, a related function also possesses non-negative definite kernel properties. This discovery has led to two significant consequences. Firstly, it refines a key inequality associated with operators in the Cowen-Douglas class, and secondly, it establishes a relationship between the reproducing kernel of certain submodules and the curvature of the associated quotient module.

Using advanced technology and analytical tools, scientists can now create detailed maps of supermassive black holes, including those at the center of our galaxy and the elliptical galaxy M87. A team of researchers predicts spectral index maps for M87* and Sgr A* by applying a complex code to simulated models of black hole accretion. Their findings indicate that the spectral index increases with stronger magnetic fields, higher electron temperatures, and greater optical depth, leading to more negative spectral index maps as radius increases. Additionally, certain regions near the event horizon exhibit positive spectral indices due to extreme plasma conditions. However, spectral index maps are sensitive to uncertainties in plasma heating, but improved understanding could allow for model discrimination using unresolved spectral indices.

Accurate predictions of uncertainty in radiation therapy treatment plans require solving particle transport problems with uncertain parameters or conditions. Monte Carlo methods are commonly used for this purpose, particularly in high-accuracy applications. However, non-intrusive solution strategies involving multiple simulations across various parameter points can be impractical due to their long computation times. In contrast, intrusive methods may be restricted by compatibility with proprietary simulation software. Our prior study demonstrated the application of a new non-intrusive uncertainty quantification technique in proton dose calculations with normally distributed errors on realistic patient data. In this paper, we present an expanded formulation of this method and delve deeper into its theoretical aspects, including bias, error, and convergence of estimates. Additionally, the approach's multivariate input model allows for flexible representation of error correlation models, which can be used to efficiently model and quantify complex, auto-correlated, and time-dependent errors within this framework.

In nonlinear optical systems, soliton molecules are key components, but producing them in mode-locked fiber lasers with precise temporal separation poses significant experimental difficulties. To overcome this challenge, we devised and implemented a novel experimental approach for harnessing the dynamics of soliton molecules within a customized laser setup. This setup utilizes second-order group-velocity dispersion and dispersion losses, with the real component maintaining a delicate balance between dispersion and nonlinearity and dispersion loss regulating the balance between gain and losses. Our experimental results confirm that by controlling dispersion loss, we can select and tailor desired temporal separations between bound pairs of soliton molecules, also enabling fine-tuning of their central wavelength and investigating associated hysteresis effects. This demonstrated regime enables the creation of multiple soliton molecules with predefined temporal separations and central wavelengths, showcasing the potential of our setup for designing innovative optical data-processing protocols.

Studying coupled oscillators with energy loss is a complex task crucial to power grid analysis, but traditional mathematical methods don't apply due to the irregular network structure resulting from energy loss. We found a significant relationship between stable synchronized states in oscillators with energy loss and a geometric property called the winding partition of their state space, which is influenced by the network layout. Using this geometric property, we developed algorithms that can compute all synchronized solutions of complex networks of oscillators with energy loss, allowing us to identify unusual behaviors of systems that lose energy as they operate. Contrary to expectations, we discovered that energy loss and loops can increase the system's ability to transfer energy, and that energy loss can even lead to multiple stable states. We applied our geometric framework to a real-world power grid simulation and identified two distinct high-voltage solutions with different energy flow patterns.

Atomistic simulations rely heavily on interatomic potentials that define the energy landscape of individual atoms. Current potentials are often tailored to limited chemical applications or lack sufficient accuracy for widespread use. A new universal potential has been developed using graph neural networks with three-body interactions, dubbed M3GNet. Trained on an extensive database of structural relaxations from the Materials Project over the past decade, the M3GNet potential enables simulations of structural relaxation, dynamics, and material properties across diverse chemical landscapes. From 31 million hypothetical crystal structures, 1.8 million materials were identified as potentially stable based on M3GNet energies. Subsequent DFT verification confirmed 1578 of the top 2000 candidates as stable, revealing a machine learning-enabled route to discovering synthesizable materials with extraordinary properties.

In 2019, researchers Qiao, Duan, and Cheng developed a distributed classification method, dividing large datasets into smaller groups, each processed by a k-nearest-neighbor classifier, with the final prediction determined by the majority vote of the group results. It was demonstrated that when k equals one and the number of groups is sufficiently large, the distributed algorithm achieves the optimal error rate with a logarithmic factor and meets the conditions for both regression and classification tasks. Essentially, distributed 1-nearest-neighbor algorithms with M groups show similar performance to standard M-nearest-neighbor algorithms. The analysis also proposed alternative methods using a refined aggregation technique, which achieved the exact minimax optimal rates.

A key aspect of delivering multimedia services in cutting-edge networks such as 5G and 6G is Quality of Experience (QoE) driven service management. This requires advanced tools for quality monitoring, forecasting, and resource management where machine learning can be instrumental. In this paper, a step-by-step guide is provided for developing and deploying QoE measurement and prediction solutions for video streaming services using supervised learning models. Initially, a comprehensive framework is presented for building and deploying supervised learning-based video streaming QoE prediction models, encompassing stages such as data collection, feature engineering, model tuning, testing, prediction, and evaluation. Secondly, the deployment of the ML model in the next-generation networks (5G/6G) using network-enabling technologies like SDN, NFV, and MEC is discussed by proposing a reference architecture. Lastly, a comparative study of the most up-to-date supervised learning ML models for QoE prediction of video streaming applications is presented based on multiple performance metrics.

The emergence of GAIL sparked significant interest in adversarial imitation learning (AIL) methods, with ValueDice being one such method that stands out. ValueDice surpasses classical Behavioral Cloning (BC) under offline conditions and requires fewer interactions than GAIL in online settings. However, we question whether the improvements seen in ValueDice are a result of more sophisticated designs. We address this inquiry by drawing the following conclusions. Firstly, we demonstrate that ValueDice can be reduced to BC under offline conditions. Secondly, we find evidence of overfitting and the importance of regularization in low-data regimes, showing that weight decay allows BC to nearly match ValueDice's performance. These findings explain ValueDice's superior offline performance. Thirdly, we show that ValueDice's effectiveness relies on having a complete expert trajectory, and when this condition is met, it becomes similar to BC, which performs well under the same circumstances. Finally, our study highlights the broader implications for imitation learning research beyond ValueDice.

To study the phenomenon of exchange bias, researchers fabricated ultrathin layers of NiFe and cobalt oxide on highly sensitive mechanical oscillators. These unique resonators could be stimulated in three dimensions, enabling the measurement of three torque components simultaneously. By analyzing the magnetic properties of the interfaces between the NiFe and cobalt oxide layers, researchers were able to confirm the presence of exchange bias at very low temperatures. Further studies revealed that the exchange bias effects persisted despite substantial "training" of the material's magnetic properties. By modeling the experimental data with established theoretical equations, researchers were able to accurately describe the behavior of the magnetic material and the effects of exchange bias.

In typical graph-based recommender systems, data is readily available at training time, but this is impractical for real-world applications where new information constantly streams in. To make the most of this continuous data, current graph-based recommendation models require frequent retraining, which is not feasible. This paper investigates a more realistic scenario - graph-based streaming recommendations - and introduces a novel, Lightweight Compositional Embedding (LCE) model that efficiently updates its predictions in real-time. LCE achieves this by learning explicit representations for a subset of nodes, while implicitly representing others based on their interactions. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation comparing LCE to competitive baselines on three large datasets under streaming conditions. The results showcase LCE's superior performance, demonstrating that it can match the best results with significantly fewer parameters.

Bayesian learning enables continuous updates of an agent's knowledge with new information.  However, direct Bayesian approaches in dynamic environments lead to slow adjustments and may inaccurately converge on key parameter values. In changing settings, a common strategy is to disregard or de-emphasize past data; yet, this simplistic forgetting mechanism overlooks the reality that many real-world situations involve revisiting similar scenarios. Our proposed BAM framework leverages past experience by allowing the agent to select which previous observations to retain and which to discard. We show that BAM encompasses numerous widely-used Bayesian methods tailored for non-stationary environments, and our experiments demonstrate the ability of BAM to effectively adapt in an ever-evolving world.

Research into neural networks' limitations when dealing with out-of-distribution data has gained prominence, but current studies mostly focus on data that can be represented in a Euclidean format. However, graph-structured data presents unique challenges, including the complex relationships between nodes and the structural information embedded within the graph, which complicates efforts to develop generalizable models. This paper tackles the out-of-distribution problem for graph-structured data by introducing a new learning approach called Explore-to-Extrapolate Risk Minimization (EERM), which enables graph neural networks to harness invariance principles for improved predictions. EERM relies on multiple context explorers, which are adversarially trained to maximize the variance of risks across multiple virtual environments. By utilizing this design, the model can effectively extrapolate from a single observed environment, even in node-level prediction tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical guarantees and real-world experiments on datasets with artificial spurious features, cross-domain transfers, and dynamic graph evolution.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have effectively tackled classification and link prediction challenges by translating data into graph representations, but existing models often rely on static graph structures, which are inadequate for highly dynamic systems with changing connectivity patterns. This limitation leads to suboptimal performance in non-stationary environments, while dynamic graph modeling can uncover system characteristics that go beyond classification capabilities. Current methods primarily focus on undirected graph generation through cross-node correlations, but this is insufficient for capturing interaction directions crucial in fields like neuroscience. In response, DECENNT, a novel neural network model, is introduced to learn directed, dynamic graphs tied to specific classification or prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms state-of-the-art methods across five tasks and yields task-specific, interpretable dynamic graphs that not only corroborate existing findings but also offer additional insights. Furthermore, DECENNT's temporal attention module can pinpoint critical time intervals essential for predictive downstream tasks from multivariate time series data, which complements functional neuroimaging data with dynamic graph representations that align with existing knowledge.

To analyze the hydrodynamic attractor in Yang-Mills kinetic theory, undergoing Bjorken expansion and Color Glass Condensate conditions, we employed principal component analysis. The hydrodynamic attractor's characteristics are dominated by a single principal component that determines the energy scale at late times. The process of reaching this state involves the decline of secondary principal components, representing pressure anisotropy deviations, screening masses, and scattering rates. Our findings indicate that for a broad range of couplings, the late-time approach to the hydrodynamic attractor can be effectively modeled using exponential decay. Furthermore, the decay rate's dependency on coupling strength translates into a straightforward relationship with the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio.

Researchers have developed self-correcting quantum memories with robust properties, offering potential for improved error correction. This study proposes a localized decoder for a color code variant, the XYZ code, achieved through local rotation of physical qubits' bases. Under ideal noise conditions, our decoder exhibits characteristics of a two-dimensional fractal code, specifically, the absence of string-like logical operators, mimicking partially self-correcting behavior at infinite dephasing bias. At low error rates, simulations indicate that memory time scales polynomially with system size, but within a system size limit that increases as error rates decrease. Although partially self-correcting behavior is unattainable at finite noise bias, our findings still reveal enhanced memory times at more realistic noise levels. Our research justifies designing localized decoders to reduce global decoding's bandwidth requirements for actual noise patterns.

Random quantum circuits have diverse applications in quantum computing, many-body systems and black hole physics, often revolving around the creation of quantum pseudorandomness by approximating unitary t-designs, which mimic Haar randomness up to a specific order (t) of moments. A groundbreaking study by Brandão, Harrow and Horodecki established that circuits of specific depth can achieve this approximation, but a recent work has refined their argument, demonstrating a lower bound on the spectral gap for local random quantum circuits, which subsequently allowed for the generation of unitary t-designs in circuits of much lower depth. This refinement involved the application of Gao's quantum union bound and the beneficial properties of the Clifford group. Additionally, a related finding showed that certain sequences of random unitaries exhibit rapid convergence to the Haar measure.

Smart home absence detection is gaining prominence as a critical application for various scenarios. Scenarios such as caring for elderly individuals, those with dementia, and home quarantine require knowing whether occupants are at home. Previous research focused mainly on using pressure/door sensors and cameras to detect when individuals leave their residences, but these methods can be intrusive and necessitate adjustments in sensor placement. Our investigation explores the potential of appliance electrical consumption as a non-intrusive indicator of occupants' presence or absence, leveraging the results of power disaggregation. Due to the unavailability of a suitable dataset, we simulated outing events on the well-established UK-DALE dataset, a standard resource for non-intrusive load monitoring. Evaluating several machine learning algorithms on this generated dataset revealed that absence detection using appliance power consumption is a viable approach.

We introduce a novel end-to-end solution for near-field Photometric Stereo, utilizing multiple closely positioned light sources. This setup is particularly beneficial for large stationary objects. Our approach boasts impressive speed, generating 3D models from 52 high-resolution images within a second on a standard GPU. This rapid performance unlocks potential applications in AR and VR technologies. In contrast, conventional methods rely on optimization in conjunction with far-field Photometric Stereo networks operating on individual pixels or small areas. However, these methods are hampered by slow processing speeds, high memory requirements, and vulnerability to noise and calibration errors. To address these limitations, we have developed a multi-resolution recursive scheme that estimates surface normals and depth maps for the entire image at each step. By leveraging the predicted depth map at each scale to estimate pixel-specific lighting for the next scale, our method significantly surpasses existing near-field Photometric Stereo reconstruction techniques in both speed and accuracy. Specifically, it achieves an almost 45 times faster execution and a 2 degree improvement in accuracy (resulting in a 11.3 degree Mean Angular Error) compared to the state-of-the-art near-field Photometric Stereo technique, which employs iterative optimization.

In recent years, advancements in light field applications, such as rendering and depth estimation, have been significant.  However, state-of-the-art light field rendering methods excel at handling semi-transparent and reflective objects, but depth estimation techniques struggle with the same complexities, often failing to deliver accurate results. We attribute this issue to conventional methods that solely rely on a single "true" depth value, disregarding the fact that multiple objects at varying depths can contribute to a pixel's color. We address this problem by exploring the concept of outputting a depth distribution, rather than a single estimate. Building on this idea, we propose several deep-learning-based approaches and introduce the first comprehensive dataset for multimodal light field depth estimation. This dataset contains the depths of all objects contributing to a pixel's color, enabling the evaluation of our proposed methods through KL divergence measurement. With our in-depth analysis and novel dataset, we aim to initiate a new direction in depth estimation research, tackling the long-standing challenges in this field.

We've compiled a comprehensive catalog of 65,981 Mira-type variable stars from the OGLE database, where nearly two-thirds (40,356) are situated in the galactic bulge fields and 25,625 are located in the galactic disk. The majority of these stars (47,532) were previously undiscovered. Our catalog includes fundamental observational parameters and extensive photometry data from the OGLE-II, OGLE-III, and OGLE-IV phases, which began in 1997. A rigorous, visually-intensive selection process, led by experienced astronomers, has resulted in a highly accurate and reliable dataset suitable for use as a machine learning training set. Our analysis indicates that this catalog has a completeness rate of approximately 96%, allowing for the comparison of Mira variable characteristics across different regions of the Milky Way, including instances where stars have evolved from semi-regular variables or vice versa. This rich dataset is ideal for studying the Milky Way's three-dimensional structure and could potentially shed light on the enigmatic X-shaped bulge.

This study presents a compact image segmentation model, L^3U-net, designed for real-time performance on edge devices with limited resources. To enhance processing efficiency, we've developed an innovative data folding technique that takes advantage of the parallel processing capabilities in CNN accelerators. Furthermore, we've implemented the proposed model on the MAX78000 device, and the outcomes demonstrate that L^3U-net achieves greater than 90% accuracy across two distinct segmentation datasets while maintaining a frame rate of 10 fps.

Utilizing lunar recession measurements from sedimentary layers and eclipses, we've made a new, model-independent measurement of the Hubble constant by analyzing the Earth's Moon recession rate. Accounting for tidal effects, we've determined the Hubble constant to be $63.01 \pm 1.79$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, which aligns with the Planck space mission's CMB measurement and is below existing local universe estimates. Our finding marks the first-ever direct, single-step measurement of the current universe expansion rate, unaffected by the systematic errors present in other methods such as type Ia supernovae or baryon acoustic oscillations. Our results provide crucial evidence that existing Hubble tension might be attributed to systematic uncertainties within the local distance ladder.

Developing automatic speech recognition systems for multiple Indic languages is difficult due to the language-specific nature of acoustic and lexical data.  The paucity of open-source datasets further exacerbates the challenge, particularly when considering multilingual approaches. In this work, we examine the effectiveness of a multilingual end-to-end ASR system relative to monolingual models trained on the output of a language identification module. By combining the decoding information from the multilingual model with language-specific models, we achieve a significant reduction in word error rates of up to 50%.  Furthermore, we propose an analogous approach for tackling code-switched scenarios, yielding WER improvements of 21.77 and 28.27 for Hindi-English and Bengali-English speech respectively. Our research highlights the potential of transformer-based models like wav2vec 2.0 in facilitating the development of multilingual ASR and code-switched ASR systems for Indic languages.

The enigma of dark matter persists, but an upcoming investigation of the early universe may uncover crucial information. Dark matter interactions could significantly impact the formation of the first stars and galaxies by altering the temperature of gas and the suppression of matter in the universe. Nevertheless, these interactions' effects on the temperature and composition of matter have not yet been taken into account. In this research, we derive the contributions of these interactions to the development of the cosmos, tracking them until the beginning of the first stars. Our findings indicate that dark matter interactions can substantially alter the large-scale temperature fluctuations and that the suppression of matter in the universe may be more pronounced than previously thought, resulting in a 5-10% reduction in matter density compared to the standard model. As a test case, we also calculated the hydrogen power spectrum from the early universe and found notable differences resulting from the changes in the gas temperature and ionization levels. We propose that these newly discovered effects must be incorporated into studies of dark matter relying on observations of the universe's early stages.

Recent advancements in learning from limited supervision have led to increased focus on developing models that can identify novel categories during testing (generalized zero-shot learning or GZSL). GZSL methods assume knowledge of all classes beforehand, with or without labeled data. However, practical applications require adaptable models that can handle the continuous addition of new seen and unseen classes in real-time (continual generalized zero-shot learning or CGZSL). A potential solution is to retrain and reuse traditional GZSL methods sequentially, but this approach suffers from significant performance degradation due to forgetting past knowledge. Recent efforts to address CGZSL have been hindered by differences in settings, practicality, and protocols, making direct comparisons challenging and limiting a clear direction forward. To address these limitations, we introduce a new, more practical and flexible Online-CGZSL setting, and a unified framework that leverages bi-directional incremental alignment to dynamically adapt to the addition of new classes, with or without labeled data, in any of the CGZSL settings. Our comprehensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in the more practical Online setting.

As dark matter research continues to gain momentum, it's essential to consider a wide range of physical processes and components to accurately predict signals, particularly those directly related to the intrinsic nature of dark matter. Our investigation focuses on the cumulative effect of dark matter subhalos and the velocity-dependent Sommerfeld enhancement of the annihilation cross-section, in both the $s$- and $p$-wave scenarios. Both factors play a significant role in the search for thermal dark matter particles with masses near or exceeding TeV, or in scenarios with a light dark sector. We provide an in-depth, analytical explanation of these phenomena and demonstrate how they scale with subhalo masses and the main Sommerfeld parameters. By deriving approximate analytical expressions for the overall boost factors resulting from these combined effects, the complex phenomenology can be better understood, leading to significantly increased gamma-ray signal predictions for a range of target masses, from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters. The presence of dark matter subhalos greatly amplifies the Sommerfeld effect, particularly on resonances, by several orders of magnitude for both $s$- and $p$-wave cases, making them crucial for producing realistic predictions.

Using a combination of $\it{Herschel}$-SPIRE and CFIS data from UNIONS, a study has identified a significant cross-correlation between the cosmic infrared background and optical background fluctuations. This correlation was observed in a combined area of $91\,{\rm deg}^2$ with a resolution of $18\,$arcsec. The analysis found a cross-spectrum with a signal detection at $\gtrsim 22\,\sigma$ that corresponds to an $r$ band brightness of $\simeq 32.5\,{\rm mag}\,{\rm arcsec}^{-2}$. However, Galactic cirrus contamination may affect these findings, particularly in areas where it accounts for up to 90% of the signal. A distinguishing feature of the observed cross-power spectrum is its shallow form $P(k)\propto 1/k$. A halo-model framework is used to interpret the results, which aligns with separate measurements of star-formation rates in galaxies. This research method has potential applications for future surveys like FYST/CCAT-prime, ${\it Euclid}$, and the Vera Rubin Observatory (LSST) to study the evolution of star formation in galaxies in greater detail.

Cyanobacteria that take on a filamentous shape, consisting of long chains of cells, are among the most ancient and thriving forms of life on Earth, exhibiting self-organized behavior in complex structures like mat-like formations and layered sedimentary deposits. Their rigid structures have proven essential to their survival and are being utilized in innovative applications such as algae-based biofuel production. In order to understand the mechanical properties that contribute to the success of these active polymers, researchers have quantified the bending stiffness of three distinct species of filamentous cyanobacteria using a laboratory device that employs fluid flow to deflect individual filaments. Additionally, measurements were taken using a highly precise testing method to determine the mechanical strength of the cell wall and its thickness. It was discovered that the stiffness of the cyanobacteria can be accurately explained by a simplified model of a flexible rod, with most of the structural stress being absorbed by a robust outer wall. Furthermore, the study connected the results to the curved shapes these microorganisms naturally form while gliding, allowing researchers to quantify the internal forces that enable them to maintain their shapes. The findings can be used to model the interactions between these filamentous cyanobacteria and their environment, shedding light on how their collective behavior arises from these interactions.

Introducing Vakyansh, an all-encompassing toolkit for speech recognition in Indic languages, designed to address the significant data and model disparities in this vast linguistic domain. With over 121 languages spoken by nearly 125 crore individuals in India, we aimed to bridge this gap by developing Vakyansh, an automated toolkit facilitating data generation, model training, evaluation, and deployment. Through Vakyansh, we generated 14,000 hours of speech data in 23 Indic languages and fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 models, ultimately creating cutting-edge speech recognition models, language models, and punctuation restoration models for 18 Indic languages. By open-sourcing these resources, our mission is to inspire the speech community to create innovative, speech-centric applications using our ASR models in Indic languages.

Current object detection methods typically use a dense approach to scan locations and scales within an image. In contrast, the latest query-based detectors transform this convention by interpreting image features through a series of trainable queries. Despite this improvement, these detectors still face slow convergence and performance limitations due to the complexity of their network design. Our research shows that the key to overcoming these challenges lies in enhancing the adaptability of decoders to match queries with diverse objects. To address this issue, we present a high-performance query-based object detector called AdaMixer, which achieves fast convergence by refining the adaptability of query-based decoding in two critical areas. Firstly, each query dynamically selects relevant image features over space and scale based on estimated offsets. Secondly, we employ an adaptive MLP-Mixer that decodes these sampled features under the guidance of each query. Thanks to these two innovative features, AdaMixer boasts an uncomplicated design without needing dense attentional encoders or explicit pyramid networks. In a challenging benchmark, AdaMixer, coupled with a ResNet-50 backbone and trained for 12 epochs, reaches 45.0 AP on the validation set, particularly achieving 27.9 AP in detecting small objects. When using a longer training scheme, AdaMixer, backed by ResNeXt-101-DCN and Swin-S, achieves 49.5 and 51.3 AP respectively. Our study introduces a straightforward, accurate, and fast-converging architecture for query-based object detectors.

Statistical physics has effectively described various physical phenomena, and now it's the ideal time to apply its principles to the culinary world. Despite the need for a scientific understanding of food categories, past theories have failed to address complex behaviors and coexistence. By combining statistical physics and thermodynamics, we've mapped the complete culinary phase space and discovered three distinct regimes: soup, salad, and sandwich. We've examined the influence of state variables on these boundaries as well as regions of coexistence and critical points, ultimately producing a definitive 3-dimensional phase diagram. With this, we can settle longstanding debates, including the question "is a hot dog a sandwich?" The answer is affirmative.

The rise in electric vehicles (EVs) and their adaptable charging schedules make them valuable assets in improving power grid performance. A transactive control framework stands out from traditional methods, such as utility-controlled or price-based charging, by offering benefits to both grid operators and customers while preserving customer autonomy. In this research, we develop a transactive electric vehicle (TEV) agent that integrates the EV owner's preference for balancing cost savings and convenience through a slider-based system, where vehicle readiness represents the owner's convenience. We also propose a private and secure bidding method that reflects the customer's transactive preferences. A transactive market mechanism is presented that combines the TEV agents with the local retail market, aligning with the current market structures for day-ahead and real-time transactions. Our results show that the proposed slider allows customers to find an optimal balance between cost savings and convenience. Simultaneously, the market mechanism effectively reduces peak prices and demand. We also compare the efficiency of Vehicle-to-Grid (V1G) and Vehicle-to-Every-Grid (V2G) technologies in relation to battery prices.

A novel approach to grounded situation recognition is presented, which involves two interactive processes for activity classification and entity estimation. The Collaborative Glance-Gaze Transformer (CoFormer) is proposed to tackle this challenging task. CoFormer comprises two modules: a Glance transformer that predicts the main activity, aided by a Gaze transformer analyzing entities and their relationships, and a Gaze transformer that estimates grounded entities by focusing on relevant entities linked to the predicted activity. Our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics on the SWiG dataset, and the training code and model weights are accessible at a provided GitHub repository.

Source extension reformulates inverse problems in wave propagation, enabling efficient solution methods in certain cases. The underlying problem in all source extension methods involves finding the source term that minimizes data errors in a least squares sense while imposing physical constraints via a penalty function. A modified version of the time reversal technique can be used to obtain an approximate solution, which can then be utilized to accelerate the convergence of iterative methods by preconditioning them. This preconditioning approach has been demonstrated to be effective in an acoustic 2D model with sources supported on a surface and constrained to a point.

We introduce a novel test-time adaptation technique for image segmentation across different domains.
Our approach, which adapts a pre-trained model at test time, relies on two key components: a learnable BatchNorm calibration module and a strong data augmentation scheme that simulates random domain shifts to learn the calibration rule.
Unlike existing domain adaptation methods, our technique eliminates the need for access to target domain data during training or computationally intensive test-time model retraining.
We demonstrate significant improvements when using our method with standard model training recipes and outperform several state-of-the-art domain generalization and one-shot unsupervised domain adaptation methods.
Furthermore, combining our approach with existing domain generalization methods yields even better results, setting a new state-of-the-art benchmark.

Light's orbital angular momentum is considered a valuable resource in quantum technology, 
utilized extensively in quantum communication and sensing. Nevertheless, the OAM state of light is 
prone to unfavorable experimental conditions, including phase distortions and varying propagation 
distances, which limits the practical application of related technologies. In this article, an advanced 
deep learning algorithm is used to detect various OAM light modes at different propagation distances 
with existing phase distortions. The trained neural network successfully identifies the topological charge 
and propagation distance of the vortex beam with high precision of 97%. This technique holds 
significant implications for the implementation of OAM-based communication and sensing methods.

Minor mergers within galaxy clusters are quite common and have the capability to produce sloshing cold fronts in the intracluster medium. Nevertheless, the resistance of these cold fronts to subsequent minor mergers remains unclear. This study aims to explore the extent to which cold fronts created by an off-center minor merger are impacted by a subsequent minor merger. We conducted 13 simulations of idealized triple cluster mergers with various approach angles and collision distances of the third cluster. All simulations showed clear cold fronts for nearly one billion years after the initial collision, with the exception of a brief period. Minor mergers occurring head-on significantly reduce the number of cold fronts, whereas those occurring off-center only slightly diminish their numbers, with outer cold fronts being particularly resilient. The findings of this research suggest that cold fronts are readily formed through minor mergers and can persist even if another minor merger occurs. As such, they are likely ubiquitous, yet determining a cluster's merger history based on its observed cold fronts may be more intricate than previously thought.
