Using these developments, we obtain expressions for the multipole moments and GW flux of compact binaries with arbitrary orbits, including the new 1.5 post-Newtonian correction. For quasi-circular orbits, we provide ready-to-use templates for detector data analysis and, uniquely, include scalar GW modes for comparison with numerical relativity results.

Two commonly used metrics, the Sackin and Colless indices, are employed to evaluate the balance of trees and validate evolutionary theories in phylogenetics. This study presents two findings related to the Sackin and Colless indices of tree structures. One discovery involves an asymptotic analysis of the average Sackin and Colless index values for binary tree shapes under a model where all shapes are equally probable. Additionally, it provides a concise and straightforward proof of a closed formula for the average Sackin index of phylogenetic trees under the same model.

We provide a microscopic analysis of four-wave mixing dressed with a control field, showcasing its capacity for managing spectral correlations at a quantum level. Beginning with a theoretical model of double Lambda configuration that incorporates a four-wave mixing process triggered by a single pump, we introduce an additional control field that interacts with the excited state, effectively creating a six-wave mixing process. This model elucidates the amplification and intensity difference squeezing enhancements arising from the interaction between the control field and the system's parameters. Furthermore, it suggests that this interaction enables the spectral management of quantum correlations between adjacent sidebands by adjusting the control field accordingly.

Demand response pricing strategies can greatly enhance power system efficiency, as well as optimize power distribution by decreasing peak consumption levels. A new pricing system, Intraday Block Pricing (IBP), is proposed to encourage consumer participation in demand response by charging for electricity based on daily time intervals. To determine IBP's associated costs, a complex optimization model is developed that aims to minimize the peak-to-average ratio while balancing the needs of both consumers and utility companies. The model is then transformed into a simpler mathematical framework and relaxed to make it easier to solve. To gauge the proposed approach's accuracy, a lower cost limit is set for the original optimization problem. Through various simulations on different case studies, it's shown that IBP results in substantial reductions in peak consumption and financial benefits for both utility companies and consumers. Additionally, simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method's solution closely matches the solution of the original problem, highlighting its effectiveness.

Geschke's work established that there exists a 3-saturated clopen graph on $2^\omega$, while also proving that no clopen graphs on $2^\omega$ have an infinite 4-saturated subgraph; conversely, an $F_\sigma$ graph exists that is $\omega_1$-saturated. Interestingly, no closed graph on $2^\omega$ is $\omega$-saturated, yet we show that for every n, there is an n-saturated closed graph on the Cantor space $2^\omega$. The key to this result lies in a probabilistic argument that underpins a key lemma, and a construction involving an inverse limit of finite graphs achieves the desired outcome.

For a permutation group G acting on a set V, a subset F of G is an intersecting set if any two of its elements map some point in V to the same image. A transitive permutation group's intersection density, denoted by ρ(G), is the maximum ratio of the size of the intersecting set to the size of its point stabilizer, over all possible intersecting sets F. A group G possesses the Erdos-Ko-Rado (EKR)-property if its largest intersecting set is its point stabilizer. This study focuses on transitive permutation groups with point stabilizers of prime order, particularly those of order 2 and 3, which lack the EKR-property. The paper presents constructions of infinite families of transitive permutation groups with a point stabilizer of order 3, achieving specific intersection densities, including 4/3 and arbitrarily large values.

To determine equilibrium emittances and damping times due to synchrotron radiation in coupled storage ring systems, we analyze how radiation impacts the normal modes of ring motion. Our approach accounts for distortions in the orbit by considering radiation emitted from off-center locations. This method involves developing and applying formulas for quick calculations, which have been integrated into the lattice design software OPA.

A galaxy known as CSS J102913+404220 has an unusual nuclear outburst, which is a peculiar event involving an energetic optical blast. A comprehensive study has been conducted on this galaxy over a decade since the outburst, incorporating various wavelength observations. We have identified a significant delay in mid-infrared flares, occurring about two months after the optical outburst, accompanied by a remarkably high peak luminosity of over 44 erg/s at 4.6 microns. This extreme luminosity is comparable to an order of magnitude higher than supernovae explosions, suggesting that the optical outburst may have been triggered by a stellar tidal disruption event. The galaxy has demonstrated significant late-time X-ray brightness, with an increase of more than 30 times the observed brightness about 100 days post-outburst, followed by a decrease of around four times within two weeks. This dramatic X-ray variability is unusual, particularly when no significant flux variations are seen in the optical, UV, and mid-infrared bands. A similar pattern of behavior has been observed in highly accreting active galaxies, potentially linked to variations in absorption. The accretion rate may induce X-ray brightening as the covering factor of the absorber decreases. Interestingly, despite the galaxy's optical continuum remaining relatively unchanged over time, an increase in the H-alpha broad emission line has been observed about a decade after the nuclear outburst, an unusual phenomenon not seen in other active galaxies. This anomaly may be attributed to the replenishment of gas clouds and their excitation within the broad line region, possibly resulting from the interaction of outflowing stellar debris with the broad line region. The study's findings emphasize the significance of the late-time evolution of tidal disruption events, which may influence the accretion properties of active galaxies as suggested by recent simulations.

Human language processing significantly influences image recognition, a phenomenon known as picture-word interference, especially in word-embedded images.  Similarly, artificial models trained jointly on text and images exhibit language-biased image classification, much like their human counterparts.  Investigating whether this bias leads to interference in image classification can shed light on the hierarchical semantic representations that artificial models derive from joint learning.  This study applies cognitive science methods to examine the biases of artificial models.  A specific benchmark task assesses how words embedded in images affect the model's classification of images across various category levels and whether this impact stems from the overlap in semantic representations between language and vision.  Our study evaluates the CLIP model using a dataset comprising word-embedded images and natural images labeled with words across different hierarchical category levels.  We found that the presence of words on images alters the model's classification of images across various category levels, yet this effect is not contingent on the semantic connection between the embedded words and images.  This suggests that, despite the word representation's strong influence over word-embedded images, it does not share a semantic connection with the image representation within the CLIP model, indicating that the CLIP model's word and image processing operate independently.

To combat pandemics such as the one triggered by COVID-19, essential tools like personal protection equipment (PPE) are needed to curb infections and shield those in close contact with patients (as noted by Heymann and Shindo, 2020, and Klompas et al., 2021). The escalating need for these products outpaces local production capabilities as the infected population grows (Ranney et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2020). Disruptions in the global supply chain caused by factory shutdowns or restricted transportation can exacerbate resource shortages (McMahon et al., 2020). In response to the COVID-19 outbreak, many regions adopted an 'our people first' stance, but this paper argues that a collaborative resource-sharing model can significantly enhance pandemic resilience. By presenting a stylized model where communities pool their resources, allowing each to access them during localized outbreaks, this approach can potentially prevent local resource depletion and minimize total infections. Our findings also suggest that the success of resource sharing relies heavily on a sufficient gap between outbreaks in different communities, underscoring the importance of pairing a global sharing mechanism with strategies to slow down infection transmission between communities. Our research marks the beginning of developing a robust global supply chain system that can effectively address future pandemics by design, rather than being confined to the current system's chance and unequal opportunities.

To address the significant cold-start issue in CTR prediction, we introduce a comprehensive Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF). VELF mitigates data sparsity-induced overfitting through dual strategies: inferring probabilistic embeddings and utilizing rich supplementary data from cold start users and ads via trainable, regularized priors. This integrated framework is trained entirely within a variational inference process. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the merits of our proposed VELF, further confirming that our adaptable priors outperform traditional fixed priors in terms of generalization ability.

For neutrino oscillation experiments employing large Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers, separating true neutrino interactions from overwhelming cosmic-ray background is a significant challenge. Traditional methods relying on computationally expensive reconstruction algorithms can be effective in background rejection but often require initial processing. This study introduces an innovative method utilizing a 3D submanifold sparse convolutional network that processes raw data from scintillation light signals within the LAr-TPCs. This technique is applied to simulations from ICARUS, the far detector of the Short Baseline Neutrino program, and the results show a significant 76.3% reduction in cosmic background while maintaining interaction selection efficiency above 98.9%. To address potential biases stemming from imperfect input data, the study proposes incorporating Domain Adversarial Neural Networks, which adapt simulated samples to mimic real data and utilize a portion for adversarial training. Through mock-data studies, the efficacy of DANNs in bias mitigation is demonstrated, yielding interaction selection efficiency performances superior to those without adversarial training.

Researchers have lately shown significant interest in LDPC codes constructed from permutation matrices, particularly with regards to circumventing short cycles in the corresponding Tanner graph and thereby achieving a high girth. This paper outlines a method to obtain such code constructions by establishing connections between cycle existence and specific number-theoretic principles, namely those related to Sidon sets, which ultimately yields examples of LDPC codes with specified girths. Furthermore, the framework is expanded to include the creation of irregular LDPC codes.

We categorize infinite singularities in three-variable degree 3 polynomials,  $ f (x_0, x_1, x_2) $, where $ f $ is a sum of three homogeneous components. Based on this classification, we compute the jump in the Milnor number of isolated singularities at infinity when moving from special to generic fibers. This work is part of a larger investigation into the global fibrations of degree 3 polynomials in $\mathbb{C}^3$, including topological analysis of their fiber classes.

We examine a modified version of the traditional Bayesian method, in which players assess their outcomes and restrictions prior to their realization. This framework effectively represents a common type of modern online advertising, where advertisers focus on their overall anticipated utility over time and their type may fluctuate over this period. Our focus is on the incentive compatibility issue associated with this Bayesian method. Under very minimal assumptions regarding the mechanism and its environment, we provide a comprehensive description of the incentive compatibility conditions using the taxation principle. Notably, our analysis reveals that the only incentive-compatible mechanisms in this context are the well-established auto-bidding mechanisms commonly employed in the online advertising industry.

Araci et al. introduced a $p$-adic extension of the Haar distribution, denoted as the $(\rho,q)$-analogue. This new distribution was then used to develop the $p$-adic $(\rho,q)$-Volkenborn integral. The author of this paper utilizes the Mahler expansion for continuous functions to prove the Radon-Nikodym theorem in the context of the $p$-adic $(\rho,q)$-distribution on $\Bbb Z_p$.

A network of agents using the previously established quantum decision theory makes decisions based on evaluating alternatives' utility, attractiveness, and information availability, leading to a combination that influences the probabilities of selecting an alternative. This interplay between these factors results in a decision-making process characterized by multiple modes. The agents interact through information exchange, encompassing two forms: direct information sharing and collectively generated societal information. The common information field, shared among agents, tends to minimize fluctuations in the probabilities over time, potentially eliminating them. For agents with short-term memory, probabilities may converge to stable values through intense oscillations, resulting in an enduring hesitation among decision-makers. Activating the information field reduces the amplitude of these oscillations and can prevent their persistence, ultimately leading to fixed limits of convergence. The phenomenon of the dynamic disjunction effect is also described.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron initially demonstrated equidistribution in shapes of certain number fields. This study replaces shapes with grids that retain more information from the number fields, with grids forming a bundle over the shape space. By examining these grids directly, we've extended their findings, proving the equidistribution of grids within their space for the number fields in question.

Conversational search research has received significant attention in Search-Oriented Conversational AI, a well-established platform that highlights the latest advancements. SCAI'21 took place online and featured a shared task focusing on conversational question answering. Notably, all participating teams relied on answer generation models, which led to an identified area of need – the evaluation of answer accuracy. To supplement automatic evaluation, we conducted two crowd-sourced experiments to collect data on answer plausibility and faithfulness. Consequently, the original conversational QA dataset was expanded with diverse correct answers generated by participating systems.

Our work involves implementing the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) operator within the linear augmented plane wave (LAPW) formalism. ACE represents the Fock exchange through a low-rank approach, preserving total energy accuracy. We found this preservation holds true in all-electron non-relativistic total-energy calculations, using the PBE0 hybrid exchange-correlation functional. Our calculations for light atoms and molecules closely align with highly accurate multi-resolution-analysis results, differing by a few micro-Hartree units. Additionally, employing high-energy local orbitals, in conjunction with ACE, enables precise Fock exchange calculations. Lastly, we utilize this implementation to compute PBE0 energy gaps in solids and compare our results with existing all-electron studies.

NGC 1566, an active galaxy, experiences recurring X-ray outbursts that can last several years. Notably, a significant X-ray outburst in 2018 saw a substantial increase in X-ray flux, exceeding the lowest recorded levels by approximately 24 times. Through the re-examination of observations taken before, during, and after this outburst, researchers confirmed the existence of a broad feature in the X-ray spectrum that could be attributed to an emission line associated with relativistic iron. This phenomenon, in conjunction with rising X-ray continuum, supports the theory that X-rays originate in a corona above an accretion disk and are reflected by the disk. Furthermore, the response time of narrow iron emission lines to changes in X-ray continuum was found to be as brief as four months, suggesting that the region where the line is produced is remarkably small. In comparison to a similar active galaxy, NGC 2992, NGC 1566 appears to have a faster rate of iron emission variation in relation to its luminosity change. The strength of the iron emission line, alongside the variability of soft X-ray excess, is also thought to be correlated with the galaxy's accretion rate, potentially due to changes in the accretion state associated with the phenomenon of a 'changing look' active galaxy.

We investigate a social learning model in which each agent selects a neighbor at random to obtain information at every time step. It is demonstrated that, despite the reduced communication, the agents are ultimately able to converge to the truth and achieve an asymptotic convergence rate comparable to traditional methods utilizing more communication. Additionally, we obtain large deviation estimates of the logarithmic belief ratios in a specific case where an agent adopts its chosen neighbor's belief.

Approximately two decades ago, Abadi and colleagues created the Dependency Core Calculus, a versatile tool for analyzing dependencies in statically-typed programming languages. The significance of dependency analysis has since become apparent, yielding numerous benefits in language design: it empowers users and compilers to enforce security measures, remove redundant code, and address other relevant issues. Our research builds upon this foundation by developing a Dependent Dependency Calculus (DDC) for dependently-typed languages, utilizing this calculus to track temporal irrelevance and facilitate more efficient type-checking and execution processes.

We investigated nonlocal dispersion compensation in broadband photon pairs transmitted over standard ITU-T G.652D fiber by precisely measuring their temporal correlations. Through our study, we achieved near-perfect compensation of dispersion by fine-tuning the photon pairs' propagation distance to match the detection apparatus' resolution limits (approximately 41.0ps). The results showed that such high levels of compensation can be achieved with manageable fiber length increments, comparable to real-world applications. Furthermore, we maintained the timing correlations down to 51ps$\pm$21ps over two separate 10km long metropolitan fiber segments.

Online food service platforms rely heavily on food reviews and recommendations.
Despite its significance, this task is complicated by diverse contexts and multiple meanings.
This study leverages deep learning methods to tackle challenges in sentiment analysis,
review tagging, and food review retrieval. A novel web-based platform, NTU Food Hunter,
is developed at Nanyang Technological University, utilizing a range of deep learning techniques.
It aids users in choosing suitable food options. Firstly, we integrate BERT and LSTM into the
platform for food review sentiment analysis. Subsequently, a POS algorithm is designed to
automatically identify noun-adjective pairs within reviews for review tagging through POS
tagging and parsing. Additionally, we employ a RankNet model to re-rank search results and
optimize the Solr-based food reviews search system. Experimental findings suggest that our
approach holds promise for addressing real-world problems.

We investigate the sensitivity of various non-classical spin states, such as those exhibiting spin-squeezing and Dicke behavior, which can be distributed across multiple spatial modes. Our analysis yields mathematical expressions for a family of these states, revealing their potential in multiparameter measurement, as well as the optimal methods to achieve the greatest sensitivity. Additionally, we examine the mode entanglement in these states, developing an entanglement witness derived from the spin-squeezing matrix. Our findings emphasize the benefits of entanglement for distributed sensing, and outline efficient protocols for estimating multiple parameters using spatially distributed non-classical spin ensembles.

Gold nanoparticles with a radius of approximately 100 nm are studied in a high vacuum environment within a quadrupole ion trap. The particles are heated through laser illumination and monitored using two key methods: measuring mass loss to estimate evaporation rates and infer temperatures, and using direct optical measurements to distinguish between the particle's liquid and solid phases based on the light it scatters. By repeatedly heating and cooling the particles across their melting points, researchers examine the relationship between heating behavior and particle size. Undercooling, where the particle remains in a liquid state below its melting temperature, is artificially induced using multi-stage laser pulses, and the degree of undercooling is investigated and compared to theoretical models.

We translated Emile Mathieu's paper "On the five-fold transitive function of 24 quantities" into English to assist our research project focused on representing $M_{23}$ as additive functions within the finite field of $2^{11}$ elements.

Our research focuses on the task of network alignment (NA), which identifies node
correspondences in two interconnected systems by analyzing both structural
components and attribute characteristics. Most existing approaches to NA have a
common limitation: they attempt to match all node pairs simultaneously without
utilizing knowledge gained from intermediate steps to improve subsequent matches.
To overcome this limitation, we introduce Grad-Align, a novel NA method that
gradually finds node pairs by leveraging the strength of easily discovered
correspondences in the early stages of the matching process. Grad-Align starts
by creating node representations for the two networks using graph neural
networks along with a custom reconstruction loss function that incorporates both
first-order and higher-order neighborhood relationships. Subsequently, nodes are
progressively matched based on dual-perception similarity metrics, including
multilayer embedding similarity and Tversky similarity, a set comparison
measure suited for networks with varying scales. To further reinforce structural
coherence, Grad-Align incorporates an edge augmentation module. Through
comprehensive experiments on real-world and synthetic data sets, we demonstrate
that Grad-Align significantly outperforms current NA methods.

Inequitable distribution of capital or resources within populations is a notable phenomenon that researchers are eager to explore. The causes and potential solutions to address this issue are of significant interest, particularly in terms of practical applications. A model of network interaction among agents is proposed to analyze and mitigate the inequality in capital distribution. By framing game outcomes as capital reduction, the goal of inequality reduction is achieved. This study investigates various interpretations of the scheme and their effects on agent behavior in terms of capital distribution, utilizing the capital-dependent Parrondo's paradox as a case study. The findings presented here offer insights into the mechanisms underlying the formation of societal inequality.

Recurrent recommender systems have achieved success in capturing users' evolving behavior over time, yet they struggle to learn from long-term patterns. As a result, RNN-based recommenders often overemphasize users' short-term preferences, a phenomenon known as recency bias that can have a detrimental impact on both long-term user satisfaction and the ecosystem's stability. In this study, we propose recency dropout, a straightforward yet potent data augmentation approach designed to mitigate recency bias in recurrent recommender systems. Our research showcases the efficacy of recency dropout through a combination of simulation studies, offline tests, and real-world experiments conducted on a large-scale industrial recommendation system.

Minimum flow decomposition, a well-known problem in Computer Science, has variants that serve as essential models in Bioinformatics, particularly in RNA assembly problems. However, due to its NP-hard complexity, most practical multiassembly tools either apply heuristics or utilize simplified, polynomial-time versions of the problem, which may not always yield optimal or perfect results. Currently, RNA assemblers use integer linear programming (ILP) to address these variants, but this approach comes with the significant limitation of having to encode a vast number of potential solution paths. Moreover, the only available exact solver for MFD is inefficient for large instances and cannot be generalized to more practical variants of the problem. This research introduces the first efficient ILP formulation for MFD, enabling a fast and exact solution to the problem, while only requiring a quadratic number of variables. Our method can efficiently solve MFD instances in under 13 seconds, both on simulated and real-world data. Furthermore, it can be easily adapted for various practical variants of the problem, including the incorporation of longer or paired-end reads, and minimizing flow errors. We envision that our findings will remove the trade-off between the complexity of multiassembly models and their tractability, and serve as the foundation for future practical RNA assembly tools.

A cosmic distance ladder appears smooth despite the Universe's lumpiness, thanks to local distance measurements that anchor supernovae observations in a perturbed space. In this context, where nearby sources provide reference points, our analysis reveals an 11% modification to standard distance calculations due to nearby inhomogeneities around an observer's location. This distortion, stemming from tidal deformations of local spacetime as indicated by the electric part of the Weyl tensor, significantly affects the calibration of Type Ia supernovae absolute magnitudes within the Hubble flow. Our findings suggest that this effect could reconcile the Type Ia supernova and Hubble constant discrepancies without invoking early or late dark energy.

The study examines the universe's behavior in a cosmological scenario where phantom energy prevails with a specific equation of state parameter. It explores the possibility of reaching the Big Rip singularity in the far-future, working within the framework of general relativity. The analysis reveals that the Big Rip singularity might be averted due to gravitational pair-production, assuming no other mechanisms are involved. Under these conditions, the universe would enter a future state characterized by a persistent and elevated Hubble rate and energy density, along with a consistently low horizon entropy. This mirrors the universe's initial state, suggesting that not only could the Big Rip be circumvented but the universe might transition into a novel inflationary phase, ultimately giving rise to the creation of multiple universes.

In inertial navigation systems, gyroscopes play a crucial role in sensing rotation.
Developing highly accurate gyroscopes that surpass classical limitations through the utilization of quantum resources has gained significant attention. Current quantum gyroscope schemes, however, are hindered by decoherence, a phenomenon known as the no-go theorem in noisy metrology. This work introduces a novel quantum-optical-gyroscope scheme that overcomes the constraints of the no-go theorem by utilizing two quantized optical fields as a quantum probe. A comprehensive analysis of non-Markovian noise reveals that the super-Heisenberg limit can be achieved when each optical field forms a stable bound state with its environment, providing a practical approach for high-precision rotation sensing in real-world noisy conditions.

A Boltzmann-Gibbs random field is defined using an exponential expression, specifically exp(-H), where H is an energy functional of field states. A new Boltzmann-Gibbs model incorporating local interactions in the energy functional is presented. These interactions are represented by a spatial coupling function, which leverages kernel-function approximations of spatial derivatives, similar to smoothed particle hydrodynamics. A particular model based on a second-degree polynomial of the Laplace operator is examined. An explicit, mesh-free expression for the spatial coupling function (precision function) is derived, utilizing the squared exponential (Gaussian) smoothing kernel. This coupling function enables the model to smoothly transition from discrete data vectors to continuum fields. The model's connections to Gaussian Markov random fields and the Mat\'{e}rn field with ν = 1 are explored.

In this study, we reexamine itinerant ferromagnetism in 2D and 3D electron systems with varying spin-orbit effects and robust electron-electron interactions. We pinpoint the specific scattering mechanisms near the Fermi surface that trigger the collapse of the ferromagnetic quantum critical point at low temperatures. In contrast to previous research, we demonstrate that such mechanisms can't be entirely eliminated even with significant spin-orbit effects. A comprehensive analysis, free from perturbative assumptions, reveals that these mechanisms always compromise the stability of the ferromagnetic quantum critical point, resulting in a first-order phase transition. Key indicators of these mechanisms can be observed through the non-analytical dependence of spin susceptibility on the magnetic field, both distant and proximal to the phase transition.

In a multi-source status update system where each source generates status update packets according to a Poisson process, served by generally distributed service times, we introduce a source-aware preemptive management policy for the M/G/1/1 queueing model. The policy allows arriving fresh packets to preempt possible packets of the same source in the system, and we derive the moment generating functions of the age of information (AoI) and peak AoI for each source. We also derive the MGFs for the source-agnostic preemptive and non-preemptive policies, which previously only had average AoI and peak AoI derived. Using the MGFs, we calculate the average AoI and peak AoI in a two-source M/G/1/1 queueing model for each policy. Numerical results demonstrate the impact of service time distribution parameters on the average AoI, showing that for a sufficiently heavy-tailed distribution, the source-agnostic preemptive policy is the most effective, and for a light-tailed distribution, the non-preemptive policy is the best choice. Our findings emphasize the significance of higher moments of the AoI.

Gaussian processes are highly effective in modeling continuous processes within machine learning and statistics. When the values of a process are known at a set of specific locations, they can be used to build an interpolating surface with a Gaussian process for predictive purposes and uncertainty analysis elsewhere. However, there are instances where the accessible information cannot be represented by a finite number of points, such as in boundary value problems that contain data on the boundaries of a region. In this study, we develop a Gaussian process model based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, enabling the combination of standard finite data with uncountable data by leveraging the equivalence of conditional expectation and orthogonal projections. This construction is explored within the context of statistical models, including computational considerations and a proof-of-concept demonstration.

The application of deep learning for liver and liver tumor segmentation in medical imaging continues to gain traction due to the increasing prevalence of liver cancer. Current network architectures have shown promise but still face significant challenges in accurately segmenting liver lesions. To address these limitations, a novel hybrid network called SWTR-Unet was developed by combining convolutional and transformer-based components. This work evaluates the performance of the proposed network on liver MRI and CT scans from the LiTS challenge, comparing it with established state-of-the-art networks and achieving superior Dice similarity scores. Furthermore, the study includes correlation analysis and ablation studies to identify factors affecting the method's accuracy, with the proposed approach showing comparable results to expert segmentations. The successful implementation of the SWTR-Unet network has the potential to reduce time and resource requirements in clinical settings.

Recent research has highlighted the vulnerability of deep neural networks to 3D adversarial attacks, particularly those targeting point clouds. Current point cloud adversarial methods, however, lack transferability and are easily defendable. To overcome these limitations, a new approach is introduced in this study, focusing on the low-frequency component of point clouds to create more effective adversarial samples by combining losses from the point cloud and its low-frequency representation. Experimental results demonstrate that this method, referred to as AOF, significantly enhances transferability compared to state-of-the-art attacks and resists state-of-the-art 3D defense techniques. Moreover, AOF-generated adversarial point clouds exhibit greater deformation than outliers compared to clean point clouds.

The effects of nuclear structure on multiplicity and anisotropic flows in isobaric collisions of $^{96}_{44}$Ru + $^{96}_{44}$Ru and $^{96}_{40}$Zr + $^{96}_{40}$Zr are studied at four different energies using the string melting version of the AMPT model. By comparing the results to recent experimental data from the STAR collaboration, it's observed that quadrupole deformation significantly influences the anisotropic flow at high central collisions, octupole deformation affects near-central collisions, and neutron skin effect dominates mid-central collisions. Furthermore, these effects are more pronounced at lower energies.

The concept of importance weighted variational inference (IWVI) is revisited as a potential strategy for learning complex models with hidden variables. This approach leverages a new set of variational bounds called Monte Carlo objectives (MCOs), which replace intractable integrals with estimates obtained via importance sampling. Building upon the work of Burda, Grosse and Salakhutdinov (2016), which demonstrated that increasing the number of importance samples improves the bound's tightness to the likelihood, this study establishes a series of results that connect properties of Monte Carlo estimates to the tightness of MCOs. In contrast to conventional wisdom, we find that smaller Monte Carlo variance does not necessarily yield better bounds, but rather, negative correlation has a more significant impact on reducing the variational gap. Furthermore, this research extends the original monotonicity theorem by incorporating non-uniform weights, offering several practical implications. Our findings draw from the theory of stochastic orders.

We analyze the behavior of a simple congestion game with two resources, modeled using a variant of the Experience-Weighted Attraction (EWA) algorithm, where a large number of agents follow this algorithm. The game is influenced by three parameters: the overall decision-making intensity $a>0$, a memory loss factor $\sigma\in [0,1]$, and an asymmetry parameter $b \in (0,1)$, which represents the proportion of agents using the first resource at equilibrium. Our study demonstrates that changes in these parameters can cause the system's behavior to switch from convergence to an equilibrium, to limit cycles, or even chaos. We show that for any given memory loss factor $\sigma$, the system will eventually destabilize when the decision-making intensity $a$ is sufficiently high. Interestingly, when memory loss is minimal ($\sigma=0$), the system often exhibits chaotic behavior, unless the network is symmetric ($b = 1/2$), while increasing memory loss ($\sigma$) can lead to the emergence of a stable, two-periodic cycle, simplifying the system's dynamics and making it more predictable. To further support our findings, we conduct simulations and create bifurcation diagrams illustrating the intricate complexity of the population dynamics in this simple congestion game.

Neural networks known as capsule networks have demonstrated promising outcomes in various computer vision tasks, but traditional capsule networks fall short in achieving state-of-the-art results on more intricate datasets due to their substantial computational and memory demands. To address this limitation, we introduce the Momentum Capsule Network (MoCapsNet), a novel architecture inspired by Momentum ResNets, which utilizes reversible residual blocks to significantly reduce memory usage. Our work outlines how these invertible blocks can be effectively integrated into capsule networks. Experimental results reveal that MoCapsNet outperforms baseline capsule networks on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets while utilizing substantially less memory, and the source code for MoCapsNet is freely available on GitHub.

To establish a framework for discussing continuity, one must first define the
properties of open sets within a space. These properties are outlined by three
fundamental axioms governing topologies, which dictate what constitutes open
sets in a given space. This paper will examine the consequences of modifying one
of these axioms on the continuity of functions.

In connected graphs, finding the optimal path necessitates identifying the least costly route through the graph's edges. Traditionally, algorithms such as Bellman Ford address this challenge by employing predefined edge costs. However, conventional planning methods fall short when edge costs need to be adjusted dynamically according to specific task requirements. To overcome this limitation, a neural network representation of pathfinding problems can be created by translating cost values into synaptic weights, enabling real-time weight adaptation through network learning. By initiating network activity and allowing it to propagate, solutions identical to those obtained through the Bellman Ford algorithm can be derived. This neural network architecture boasts the same computational complexity as Bellman Ford while also enabling learning mechanisms, such as Hebbian learning, to adapt weights and refine paths in response to changing task demands. This novel approach is demonstrated through applications in obstacle avoidance and sequential path navigation, thereby offering a promising new paradigm where path augmentation and finding are seamlessly integrated.

The existence of the axion particle remains uncertain, yet the concept of the axion field has been employed to develop a localized model of a U(1) gauge theory that incorporates both classical and quantum gauge invariance. Recent introductions of non-abelian analogues of axion fields, accompanied by their unique symmetries, enable analogous construction of non-abelian chiral gauge theories. As seen in previous instances, the gauge symmetry is disrupted, resulting in the mass acquisition of the gauge boson through the absorption of axions, rendering them non-physical in this context.

We focus on four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories that exhibit S-confinement, making them equivalent to a Wess-Zumino model. Classification exists for theories with simple gauge groups and S-confining dualities in this category. Our proof encompasses S-confining dualities where matter fields belong to rank-$1$ and/or rank-$2$ representations, based solely on S-confining dualities for $SU(N)$ with $N+1$ flavors and $Usp(2N)$ with $2N+4$ fundamentals. To achieve this, we apply a series of deconfinements followed by re-confinements, carefully monitoring the explicit superpotential at each step.

We investigate the local and bipartite entanglement properties of a free Fermi gas in thermal equilibrium within a multi-dimensional Euclidean space, specifically focusing on the thermal R\'enyi entropies with a given index. The entanglement entropies are shown to be positive for temperatures greater than zero, with certain R\'enyi indices not exceeding 1. Moreover, the asymptotic behavior of these entanglements is analyzed for large temperatures and a scaling parameter, both under conditions of fixed chemical potential and fixed particle density, thereby providing a key proof for previously published temperature results.

The discrete Fourier transform holds crucial significance in photonic quantum information processing. However, its applicability in high-dimensional contexts relies heavily on the physical encoding used. A novel approach in emerging platforms, such as frequency bins, involves incorporating additional radio-frequency harmonics to enable scalable discrete Fourier transforms. This method has been numerically proven effective up to d = 10, with an experimentally implemented demonstration of d = 3, showcasing potential applications in high-dimensional quantum communication and networking protocols.

This paper builds upon our previous research of spherical representations in the context of operator algebras, introducing analogous concepts of dimension groups using operator systems. It then extends this study to the inductive limits of compact quantum groups and establishes a quantum analogue of Olshanski's spherical unitary representations, thus validating Ryosuke Sato's approach to asymptotic representation theory for quantum groups.

A widely used approximation of the Klein-Gordon equation for a real scalar field with mass $\mu$ within a Kerr black hole's geometry, originally obtained by Detweiler, has a confirmed mistake in a factor of $1/2$, first noted by Pani. The correction reveals unusual properties challenging a common approach. We rectify this issue by incorporating the next-to-leading order (NLO) contribution, showing it significantly reduces the numerical error of the leading order solution. For the majority of $r_g\mu$ values, the percentage error is less than $10\%$, especially when $r_g\mu \lesssim 0.35$. Additionally, the NLO solution has a simpler form, making it more practical for use.

The task of natural language inference (NLI) is gaining significant importance in the context of natural language understanding, which necessitates determining the relationship between paired sentences (premise and hypothesis). Recent studies have utilized contrastive learning by drawing upon NLI datasets to learn sentence representations, yet they mainly focus on comparisons based on sentence-level representations. This paper presents a Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning approach (PairSCL), which incorporates a cross-attention module to learn joint representations of sentence pairs. PairSCL employs a contrastive learning objective that distinguishes varied sentence pair classes by pulling similar pairs together and pushing apart dissimilar ones. PairSCL outperforms other methods on average by 2.1% on two public NLI datasets. Moreover, our method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art method in seven transfer tasks of text classification.

The "isobar run," also known as RHIC, was developed to investigate how collisions of $^{96}_{40}Zr$ and $^{96}_{44}Ru$ impact various observables, ultimately to isolate $Z$-dependent effects. Contrary to expectations, STAR data demonstrated that these two isotopes exhibit significantly different properties, resulting in observable differences that surpass charge-dependent variations. Despite numerous studies examining their shape discrepancies in relation to various parameters, a general understanding is that their distinct characteristics can be attributed to nuclear structure, specifically the properties of their lowest excited states. Nonetheless, a precise link between low-energy and high-energy nuclear physics remains elusive. This paper aims to establish such a connection by utilizing thermal density matrices of preheated nuclei, with effective temperature serving as a parameter for determining which set of excited states to incorporate into calculations. Additionally, I propose the application of a semiclassical "flucton" method at finite temperatures to compute thermal density matrices.

We propose a probabilistic binary latent variable model that can identify and model approximate patterns in binary data with high noise levels. This model is an adaptation of the Noisy-OR model, which was originally applied in disease and topic modeling. The model's capabilities were showcased through the discovery of underlying patterns in retinal neuron recordings and can be applied broadly to reveal latent structures in binary data corrupted by noise. In the context of neural data analysis, the model aims to explain individual neuron spikes by associating them with cell assemblies - groups of neurons that fire together due to interactions or other factors. The model infers sparse activity patterns within binary latent variables, each representing the activity of a cell assembly, and updates the conditional probability kernels of the model components through an expectation maximization process that learns from the data. Our model's performance is evaluated using synthesized spike trains that mimic real retinal responses to various stimuli, and we also apply it to actual retinal ganglion cell recordings to explore the underlying structure.

We investigate a 3D ternary system, which is a sharp-interface limit of a model derived from the Nakazawa-Ohta density functional theory of triblock copolymers, combining an interface energy term with long-range interaction effects. While binary systems in 2D and 3D, and ternary systems in 2D have been extensively studied, little is known about the ternary system in 3D. Specifically, it remains unclear whether minimizers are composed of a finite number of components. This paper offers a positive response to this query by demonstrating that the number of components in a minimizer is limited by a value determined solely by the total masses and interaction coefficients. A key obstacle is the 3D structure, which prevents the separation of the long-range interaction term from the perimeter term, thereby rendering the actual shape of minimizers unknown, even in cases of small masses. This uncertainty stems from the lack of a quantitative isoperimetric inequality with two mass constraints in 3D, complicating the construction of competitive systems.

A novel communication approach has been introduced, focusing on transmitting data for AI tasks with limited concern for image quality. However, some applications like self-driving cars necessitate a balanced evaluation of image clarity and AI performance. To address this issue, a proposed framework, TOSC-SR, aims to minimize semantic-level distortions and pixel-level imperfections simultaneously, posing a new rate-distortion optimization challenge. A novel distortion metric based on the mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels enables the evaluation of semantic-level loss. By deriving an analytical solution and determining the optimal mapping, TOSC-SR overcomes existing limitations. Additionally, a variational approximation of mutual information is used to extend TOSC-SR's applicability to multiple AI tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of TOSC-SR over traditional image communication systems and deep learning-based benchmarks in terms of image quality, AI performance, and generalizability.

For a given polynomial p, the degree of the resulting Chebyshev's method, C_p, is examined. Specifically, when p is a cubic polynomial, the degree of C_p can be either 4, 6, or 7. We investigate the dynamics of C_p in these cases. It is proven that for cubic polynomials that are either unicritical or non-generic, the Julia set of C_p is connected. Furthermore, the family of rational maps obtained from applying Chebyshev's method to a non-unicritical, generic cubic polynomial is parameterized by the multiplier of one of its extraneous fixed points. We denote a member of this family with multiplier λ as C_λ. Notably, the Julia set of C_λ is found to be connected whenever λ falls within the interval [-1, 1].

Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder impacting people of all ages globally. As an alternative treatment for epilepsy patients who have unsatisfactory results with medications or surgery, Deep Brain Stimulation has gained attention. To improve DBS procedure planning and standardization, it is crucial to develop an algorithm for automatically pinpointing the DBS stimulation target - specifically, the Anterior Nucleus of Thalamus. This task is particularly challenging. Our research compares and evaluates various methods for ANT-DBS localization, including traditional and AI-driven approaches such as heatmap matching and DSNT. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that machine learning-based localization methods, utilizing pseudo labels during training, can match inter and intra-rater variability and are significantly faster than traditional methods.

The dynamics of 2D truncated Airy waves and three-component solitons within a system driven by coupled fundamental-frequency and second-harmonic fields through quadratic terms have been explored. The system models optical media and Bose-Einstein condensate mixtures and supports stable solitons alongside exact, stable truncated-Airy-wave states in a single fundamental-frequency component. Moreover, it's feasible to introduce vorticity into 2D Airy modes. By running comprehensive simulations, we investigate interactions between originally separate, oppositely directed, truncated Airy waves in the second-harmonic field, which result in the merging of input into narrow soliton pairs, as opposed to the 1D system's behavior where the interacting Airy waves split into multiple solitons. Interactions between Airy waves carrying identical vorticities produce additional soliton pairs, whereas opposite vorticities yield small-amplitude debris. Collisions involving slowly moving solitons with a heavy Airy wave involve bounces back for the former, absorption for the latter, and quasi-elastic collisions for faster solitons. Furthermore, soliton-soliton collisions may either lead to single-mode mergers or elastic passage for lower and higher velocities, respectively.

Under mechanical stress, amorphous solids exhibit a susceptibility to plastic responses.
Studies on amorphous granular systems revealed that plastic events, characterized by quadrupolar behavior, can suppress elastic responses.
In dense quadrupole configurations, the quadrupole field's gradients generate emergent dipole sources, resulting in distinct alterations to the mechanical response, evident in displacement field variations.
This paper investigates the impact of screening in classical glass formers comprising point particles interacting via binary forces.
The analysis of inverse power law and Lennard-Jones interactions demonstrates that both cases exhibit strong screening of the elastic response, consistent with the underlying theory.
A novel measure quantifying the degree of deviation from classical elasticity theory is proposed and shown to be functionally linked to the energy lost due to plastic responses.

A branching program model with $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear query forms is used to simulate a natural model of read-once linear branching programs. This model is restricted in two ways, resulting in the weakly and strongly read-once models, both of which are generalizations of read-once branching programs and parity decision trees. The key findings in this context are two-fold. Firstly, a new pseudo-random class of functions, referred to as directional affine extractors, is defined, which has been proven to be difficult to solve on average for the strongly read-once model. An explicit construction of these functions with favorable parameters is presented, thus extending previous research by Cohen and Shinkar (ITCS'16), which showed average-case hardness for parity decision trees. Additionally, a stronger version of affine extractors is introduced, which could have independent value due to its importance. Secondly, the $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ proof system is explored, which is an extension of the resolution method with linear queries. It is demonstrated that a linear branching program can be used to define a proof system, and conversely, that a weakly read-once linear BP solving a search problem can be converted to a $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ refutation with a constant factor increase in complexity.

A novel, two-stage method is presented for creating and evaluating approximation algorithms using Lyapunov functions. In the first stage, Lyapunov functions serve as inputs, resulting in continuous-time algorithms with a guaranteed approximation ratio. The second stage then converts these algorithms into discrete-time versions, retaining a similar approximation ratio and a provable time complexity. Notably, our method only requires the parametric form of the Lyapunov function, which is determined during the first stage by maximizing the approximation ratio of the continuous-time algorithm. The Lyapunov function approach has several advantages: it simplifies the design and analysis of various algorithms, provides a systematic framework for developing new ones, and offers new insights for enhancing existing methods. This approach is demonstrated using several submodular maximization problems.

A set of collections is considered intersecting if any pair of sets within the collection shares a non-empty overlap. A set of collections \(\mathcal{C}\) possesses the Helly property if any intersecting subset of \(\mathcal{C}\) contains a non-empty overlap. A graph can be classified as /Helly/ if the collection of its maximal complete subgraphs adheres to the Helly property. The following theorem states that for a k-regular graph with n vertices, where n surpasses a certain threshold defined by the inequality n>3k+sqrt(2k^2-k), its complement graph \bar{G} is not Helly. Furthermore, this text touches on the question of whether the properties of Hellyness and convergence under the clique graph operator are equivalent for the complement of k-regular graphs for small k.

We re-examine a problem concerning a local scale symmetry, or alternatively known as the Weyl symmetry, and demonstrate that its associated Noether current consistently equals zero. Utilizing the second Noether theorem for a local symmetry, we establish that the Noether current of the Weyl symmetry is generally vanishing in all Weyl invariant gravitational theories in four-dimensional Riemannian geometry. Furthermore, we clarify the underlying cause: the Weyl transformation is non-dynamical because it doesn't include a derivative term of the transformation parameter in contrast to conventional gauge transformations. We then extend this finding to a quantum theory of general Weyl invariant gravity and compute currents associated with choral symmetry, a specific $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry.

For autonomous driving, accurate detection of 3D objects is a critical task. Recent advances in point cloud-based detection have shown promising results, thanks to their ability to provide detailed depth information. The nuScenes dataset, provided by NuTonomy, surpasses other popular datasets such as KITTI in terms of size, sensor modalities, and annotated objects, but suffers from a significant imbalance in classes. To address this issue, a novel augmentation and sampling strategy, presented in the Class-balanced Grouping and Sampling paper, can be applied. Nonetheless, the localization precision of the model is compromised by the loss of spatial information in downscaled feature maps. To enhance the performance of this model, a detachable auxiliary network is proposed, which utilizes the structure information of the 3D point cloud to improve localization accuracy. This auxiliary network is trained using two point-level supervision methods - foreground segmentation and center estimation - and does not add any extra computation during inference, as it can be detached at test time.

Our Aegis Combat System implementation utilizes command and control, with key components including missile guidance and tracking. To delve deeper into the system's mechanics, a simplified model of the Aegis Combat System will be developed. In this model, a small-scale autonomous car will track a remote-controlled counterpart. The model consists of the controller and two cars, allowing the team to showcase real-world command and control features such as command, communication, and sensor data integration. An accompanying image, represented as Figure 1, illustrates the Aegis Combat System.

Research-backed decision-making theories such as Fuzzy-Trace Theory imply that people primarily focus on the essential meaning of information when making decisions. This research describes the development of GisPy, a free, Python-based software tool for assessing the Gist Inference Score in written text. By evaluating GisPy on news and scientific articles from three separate datasets, our results show that the scores generated by this tool can effectively identify documents that convey high and low levels of essential meaning. The tool can be accessed and used at its dedicated GitHub repository.

Deep neural classifiers in weakly supervised text classification typically rely on noisy pseudo-labels for training. Since these pseudo-labels are generated using heuristics, their accuracy significantly impacts performance. Selecting high-quality pseudo-labels is essential, and a seemingly simple approach is to use softmax probabilities. However, experiments demonstrate that this strategy is flawed due to poorly calibrated models producing overconfident predictions. Notably, research suggests that neural networks first learn samples with clean labels and then those with noisy labels. Motivated by this insight, a novel pseudo-label selection method, LOPS, has been proposed. LOPS takes into account the learning order of samples, hypothesizing that earlier-learnt samples are more likely to have incorrect labels. As shown in experiments on multiple real-world datasets, LOPS serves as a robust performance-boosting component for most existing weakly-supervised text classification methods.

There are several reasons why determining the faithfulness of an explanation is beneficial, including trust, understanding how the model works, and pinpointing its mistakes. For this purpose, our approach centers on the NLI task and presents a novel method called Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals. It begins by creating a counterfactual hypothesis based on the logical rules within the explanation and then checks if the model's prediction aligns with those rules (i.e., if the generated formula can logically hold true). Unlike existing methods, this approach does not require training an additional model for verification. First, we verify the effectiveness of automatically generating counterfactual hypotheses using a few-shot learning method. Next, we demonstrate that our proposed metric can distinguish between human and model agreement or disagreement on new hypothetical scenarios. Furthermore, we perform an analysis to confirm that our metric reacts to explanations that lack faithfulness.

Our research focuses on the transfer of angular momentum from guided photons to a two-level atom with an electric quadrupole transition near an optical nanofiber. We found that the generation of the axial orbital torque exerted by the driving field on the atom is determined by internal-state selection rules for quadrupole transitions and the conservation of angular momentum. The torque depends on the photon's angular momentum, the change in the atom's internal state, and the quadrupole transition's Rabi frequency. Numerical calculations were performed to determine the torques for the quadrupole transitions between specific sublevels of a $^{87}$Rb atom. The results showed that the torque for higher-order modes is larger than that for fundamental modes, except when the transition involves a specific case where the higher-order mode's torque is zero.

Our investigation into the mixing of the isoscalar pseudoscalar meson $\eta$ and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ within the framework of QCD at the $N_f=2$ level with a pion mass of $m_\pi\approx 350$ MeV reveals a precise $\eta$ mass of $m_\eta=714.1(5.4)$ MeV. This $\eta$ mass value can be correlated to its $SU(3)$ equivalent using the Witten-Veneziano relation, which yields an estimated mass of approximately 935 MeV. Utilizing a large set of gauge ensembles and correlators calculated via the distillation method, we have been able to determine the $\eta-G$ mixing energy to be $|x|=107(14)$ MeV and the mixing angle $|\theta|$ to be $3.47(46)^\circ$. It has also been found that the $\eta$ mass can be accurately derived from $\eta-\eta_c$ correlators, where $\eta_c$ represents the pseudoscalar charmonium. Our results demonstrate that the $\eta-G$ mixing effect is negligible and that the majority of the $\eta$ mass can be attributed to the topology-induced interaction arising from the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly.

The effectiveness of goal-oriented dialogue systems in achieving users' objectives is dependent on how humans perceive them as helpful. Notably, research on this aspect has been lacking. In this study, we focus on developing computational metrics to evaluate the helpfulness of dialogue systems. Initially, we established a framework for assessing helpful dialogue responses based on three key criteria: relevance, coherence, usefulness, and informativeness. Using this framework, we gathered human feedback on dialogue system helpfulness and trained a machine learning model to automatically assess responses. Furthermore, we introduced a novel approach to evaluate a dialogue system's fairness by analyzing its helpfulness towards different types of user inquiries. Our experiments on cutting-edge dialogue systems under diverse information-seeking contexts revealed an unexpected bias, with existing systems performing better on queries related to developed countries, highlighting potential fairness concerns in the current generation of goal-oriented dialogue systems.

In recent years, a rise in point cloud-based representations has occurred, which have become increasingly detailed but still struggle to produce ordered sets of points. Our novel sampling approach, inspired by spherical scanners, introduces Spotlights, a model representing 3D shapes through a compact 1D array of depth values. By simulating cameras on a sphere, we capture sample points as potential intersections with objects using light rays, thus generating a structured point cloud implicitly defined by depth. Our detailed analysis of this sampling scheme proves its effectiveness for point cloud completion and our experiments demonstrate its competitive accuracy, consistency, and reduced computational cost. Furthermore, we show superior results for point cloud registration compared to state-of-the-art completion methods.

Research has shown that large language models can be vulnerable to privacy risks due to data memorization during training, with many recent studies focusing on the pre-training phase. In contrast, the fine-tuning phase has received limited attention, and there is still a lack of understanding regarding how various fine-tuning methods impact data memorization. As the pre-training and fine-tuning approach becomes increasingly popular, this is becoming a growing concern. This paper conducts an empirical investigation of memorization risks in fine-tuning methods using membership inference and extraction attacks, revealing significant differences in their susceptibility to these threats. Our findings indicate that fine-tuning the model's head makes it particularly susceptible to attacks, while fine-tuning smaller adapters appears to be less vulnerable to known extraction attacks.

A new class of techniques, termed lightweight fine-tuning methods, achieves efficient transfer learning by adjusting only a few additional parameters, while leaving the pre-trained model's parameters unchanged. Although proven to be a successful method, there is a lack of research regarding how the downstream fine-tuning approach should influence the pre-training stage. This work demonstrates that taking the optimal choice of fine-tuning method into account enhances the performance of parameter-efficient fine-tuning. By utilizing meta-learning based on optimization using an adapted version of MAML, we fine-tune the pre-trained model specifically for efficient fine-tuning, resulting in improvements of up to 1.7 points in cross-lingual NER fine-tuning. Our experiments and analysis confirm that the modifications introduced in MAML are critical for the achieved gains.

At the Paul Scherrer Institut's High Intensity Proton Accelerator (HIPA) cyclotron, a continuous 590 MeV proton beam is produced at a maximum power of 1.42 MW. This beam is then transmitted to two target stations through a 120 meter long channel where it's used to generate surface muons before depositing its remaining energy at the SINQ spallation target for neutron production. As part of the High Intensity Muon Beamline feasibility study, researchers will replace the existing target with a thicker one to boost surface muon production, but face the challenge of minimizing proton beam losses, which can be achieved by improving their understanding of losses along the beamline through a novel approach. This approach aims to correlate experimental data from temperature and beam profile measurements, beam current readings, with Monte Carlo simulations to calculate combined power deposition and primary beam losses.

In 1984, Gauduchon analyzed a functional that represents the $L^2$-norm of torsion on a compact Hermitian manifold. He derived the Euler-Lagrange equation for this functional and found that in two-dimensional manifolds, critical metrics are characterized by balancedness, which implies a vanishing torsion 1-form. This note extends Gauduchon's result to higher dimensions, demonstrating that critical metrics are indeed balanced across all dimensions. Furthermore, this note also explores the $L^2$-norm of the full Chern torsion and provides examples that show critical points of this functional do not necessarily correspond to K\"ahler metrics.

Our research investigates how the eccentricity of binary neutron star systems affects the accuracy of gravitational wave parameter estimation. Using signals with low eccentricity detected by the advanced LIGO sensitivity, we employ a Bayesian approach with a circular waveform model and identify biases in recovered intrinsic parameters such as the chirp mass, mass ratio, and tidal deformability. By comparing these results to those obtained using the Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method, we establish the conditions under which this analytical approach is valid. We then apply this method to a realistic population of binary neutron star sources and find that measurement errors and biases in the estimated parameters increase with eccentricity. These biases are primarily dependent on eccentricity rather than component masses, leading to narrow distributions in the eccentricity-bias plane. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the importance of including eccentricity in parameter estimation to avoid incorrect predictions of neutron star properties, highlighting potential biases such as posterior bimodality.

VisDial is a challenging task that involves answering a series of questions based on an image while considering the previous conversation context. Current methods have relied on supervised learning or pre-training using related datasets, but this paper presents a semi-supervised learning approach called Generative Self-Training (GST) that utilizes unlabeled web images to significantly increase the training data. GST first identifies relevant images using out-of-distribution detection and then generates hypothetical conversations associated with these images through multimodal text generation. It then trains a dialog agent on a large dataset of both real and synthetic conversations, effectively increasing the training data by up to an order of magnitude. To improve training stability, GST employs perplexity-based data selection and multimodal consistency regularization. Experimental results demonstrate that GST achieves new state-of-the-art performance on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets, with particularly significant gains in low-data regimes, achieving up to 9.35 absolute points improvement in NDCG.

To combat noise in inaccessible quantum bits, spectator qubits are employed as noise-detecting tools. These sensitive qubits, which are frequently measured, can correct errors in the primary data qubits using the collected results. For instance, when mitigating the effects of random telegraph noise-induced dephasing, a Bayesian strategy utilizing linear transformations is implemented, resulting in an optimal adaptive protocol for measurement and control. This approach effectively reduces the decoherence rate, demonstrating that the use of spectator qubits can be highly effective in the appropriate context.

Text generation systems often produce inaccurate output. In D2T systems, generating reliable information is critical for real-world applications. We present R2D2, a framework that addresses inaccurate text generation in D2T systems by training a model to both generate text and assess its credibility, along with additional detection and learning tasks. To enable this training, we developed methods for creating unfaithful text samples. Since poor entity retrieval capabilities can lead to inaccurate text generation, we introduced new metrics that focus on named entity recognition to evaluate D2T output. Our experiments show that R2D2 systems significantly improve the accuracy of generated text, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets, including FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo.

This thesis aims to investigate and scrutinize potential vulnerabilities within the Iota network 2.0 by analyzing its attack pathways. The research involves examining existing threats targeting Distributed Ledger Technologies and determining their relevance to the Iota 2.0 protocol. A targeted vulnerability is proposed that compromises honest participants' ability to write to the ledger, and its effects are studied within a network comprising nodes running full-node software.

The development of image captioning models capable of processing numerous languages has been hindered by the absence of suitable evaluation datasets. We introduce the Crossmodal-3600 dataset, which consists of 3600 geographically diverse images annotated with human-written captions in 36 languages. These images were collected from regions worldwide where the respective languages are spoken, and captions were created to ensure uniformity in style across languages while avoiding direct translations that could introduce bias in the annotations. Our results demonstrate that using the Crossmodal-3600 dataset yields better correlations with human assessments when selecting and evaluating massively multilingual image captioning models.

We introduce FLEURS, an n-way parallel speech dataset spanning 102 languages, created on the FLoRes-101 benchmark, with 12 hours of speech data per language. FLEURS serves as a versatile platform for evaluating universal speech representations in tasks such as ASR, Speech LangID, translation, and retrieval. This paper presents baseline performance using mSLAM and other pre-trained multilingual models. FLEURS aims to enhance speech technology for more languages and drive research in low-resource speech understanding.

The existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the given partial differential equation can be proven within Muckenhoupt weighted L_p-spaces for pseudo-differential operators. These operators are time-measurable, defined as the inverse Fourier transform of a product of a symbol and the Fourier transform of the function. The sufficient conditions for the well-posedness of the equation involve the symbol, particularly its smoothness with respect to its argument. Specifically, it can be shown that a solution u to the equation satisfies the following regularity estimates, assuming the symbol satisfies certain properties related to the weight used in the L_p-space. A constant N exists, such that the integral of the p-th power of a specific derivative of u over space and time is bounded by the integral of the p-th power of the function f over space and time. A similar inequality holds when integrating over space and time for a specific weighted p-th power of u and f. The weights are characterized by the exponents and parameters involved.

The limitations of event extraction (EE) are primarily due to data scarcity and
imbalance, but a proposed self-training framework can overcome these issues. This
framework, which we term STGG, combines two models: (1) an initial base event
extraction model that's first trained on existing annotations and then applied to
unlabeled data to identify new event mentions, and (2) a scoring model that uses
the relationships between event triggers and arguments in an Abstract Meaning
Representation graph to evaluate the accuracy of predictions. The framework uses
these predicted events, along with their associated accuracy scores, as pseudo
labels to improve the base model's performance, and guides its gradients with the
accuracy scores. The effectiveness of STGG is demonstrated through experiments on
multiple datasets, including ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN, which show a maximum
improvement of 1.9 F-score over standalone base models. Furthermore, STGG can be
applied to a range of base models and even performs well when high-quality AMR
annotations are unavailable, allowing it to leverage large amounts of unlabeled
data to enhance model performance.

The cartoon domain has seen growing interest lately. Research efforts in applying quality portrait stylization to the cartoon domain have been met with difficulty due to unresolved key constraints, including a dependency on a significant quantity of training images and a lack of ability to represent cartoon faces at an abstract level. A recent layer-swapping technique has been used to address the image quantity issue, but its usage remains restricted by lingering problems. We present a new method called Cross-domain Style mixing in this study, which combines the latent codes of two distinct domains. This method efficiently transforms faces into different cartoon characters at various levels of face abstraction using a single generator and without requiring an excessive number of training images.

Multilingual open-domain QA systems that rely on retrieved documents and
answer-span selection often face inconsistencies when dealing with documents
in various languages, due to the differing information these documents offer
on the same topic. We investigate how the biased availability of information
and cultural influences impact multilingual QA systems by examining the
behavior of retrieval models. Our analysis focuses on whether different
retriever models yield different passages given the same question across
different languages in the TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA datasets, two multilingual
question-answering datasets. We suspect that content variations in documents
across languages may stem from cultural differences and social biases.

A new approach has been developed to build a precise test for evaluating any combination of hypotheses in high-dimensional linear regression. This approach can be integrated into existing multiple testing methods to provide confidence statements on relevant predictor variables. It functions by generating test statistics for individual hypotheses through data resampling and a variable selection technique, and then combines these statistics to test any subset of hypotheses. The resulting method is highly adaptable, allowing various selection techniques and combination methods to be used. The approach is presented in two forms: a precise method and a faster, approximate version that is more suitable for high-dimensional data. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulations and analysis of real-world data, specifically gene expression data.

Current machine translation models continue to face difficulties with complex inputs, such as corrupted data and uncommon phrases and words. Several studies have attempted to address these robustness issues by categorizing types of noise and variations, then adjusting models to excel at processing them. One under-examined category involves slight nuances in meaning (non-typographical errors) that maintain the intended meaning in the target language. This category is referred to as Natural Asemantic Variation (NAV) and is investigated in the context of machine translation robustness. Our research finds that existing machine translation models perform poorly on NAV data, but we demonstrate methods to enhance their performance on NAV by retraining them with variations generated by humans. Furthermore, our results show that improving robustness to NAV can be applied across languages and that artificially generated perturbations can achieve some but not all the benefits of natural NAV data.

Mathematical methods such as integration, gradient descent optimization, and state estimation, which rely heavily on linear algebra, are generally limited to state vectors within Euclidean spaces when implemented in their standard form. This article explores how these techniques can be adapted for non-Euclidean state vectors, including those containing rotational and translational data from rigid bodies. To facilitate this, the article delves into the properties of SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups, specifically focusing on the various representations of rigid body rotations and motions, their tangent spaces, and the necessary Jacobians for employing calculus-based methods such as Runge-Kutta, Gauss-Newton minimization, and extended Kalman filter (EKF).
